subject: Communicative English
question: Define communication. List the 7 Cs of effective communication.
answer_html:
Definition Communication is the process of sharing information, ideas and feelings between two or more people so that they understand each other. The word comes from the Latin communis, meaning "common".

The 7 Cs of effective communication

  1. Clear – one idea at a time, in simple words
  2. Concise – brief, without unnecessary words
  3. Concrete – specific facts and figures ("Take one tablet after breakfast", not "Take it sometimes")
  4. Correct – accurate facts, grammar and spelling
  5. Coherent – logical and well connected
  6. Complete – all the information the receiver needs
  7. Courteous – polite, respectful and friendly

subject: Communicative English
question: Differentiate between verbal and non-verbal communication.
answer_html:
Introduction Messages are sent through words and also without words.

Verbal communication Non-verbal communication
uses words – spoken or written uses body language – no words
e.g. talking, lectures, telephone calls, letters, reports e.g. facial expression, eye contact, gestures, posture, touch, tone of voice, silence, appearance
mostly conscious and planned often unconscious and spontaneous
clear, can be recorded may be misunderstood; differs with culture
conveys facts and ideas conveys feelings and attitudes

Nursing point: patients often trust the nurse's non-verbal message more than her words, so a smile and a calm voice must match what she says.

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain the communication roles of listeners, speakers, readers and writers as health care professionals.
answer_html:
Introduction A nurse communicates all day – with patients, relatives, doctors, colleagues and the community. She plays four communication roles: listener, speaker, reader and writer. Each role needs special skills, because a small misunderstanding in a hospital can harm a patient.

1. The nurse as a listener

  • Listens to the patient's complaints, fears and needs – "Sister, I feel giddy when I stand up"
  • Listens to doctors' orders, handover reports, telephone messages and announcements
  • Uses active and empathetic listening – full attention, eye contact, nodding, not interrupting
  • Listens to tone and feelings, not only words
  • Clarifies doubts – "Do you mean the pain started after lunch?"
  • Good listening gives an accurate nursing history and prevents errors in carrying out orders

2. The nurse as a speaker

  • Greets and introduces herself; explains procedures and hospital routines
  • Gives health education to patients, families and community groups
  • Reports the patient's condition to doctors and seniors (using SBAR)
  • Gives instructions to junior staff and students
  • Speaks clearly, politely and in simple words, in the patient's language; avoids jargon
  • Uses the right tone, speed and volume; checks understanding by feedback

3. The nurse as a reader

  • Reads doctors' orders, prescriptions, case sheets and investigation reports carefully
  • Reads drug labels – name, strength, expiry date – before giving medicines (reading errors cause medication errors)
  • Reads charts and graphs – TPR charts, intake–output charts, partographs
  • Reads circulars, policies, textbooks, journals and research articles to update knowledge
  • Uses skimming and scanning to find information quickly, and careful (intensive) reading for drug orders

4. The nurse as a writer

  • Writes nursing notes, care plans, reports (shift, incident, transfer), patient history and discharge instructions
  • Writes letters, applications, indents, requisitions and emails
  • Writes health education material – leaflets and posters
  • Writing must be legible, accurate, brief, objective, dated, timed and signed, in correct grammar and approved abbreviations
  • In advanced roles – writes research papers and abstracts

Importance of these roles

  • Patient safety – correct understanding of orders and drug labels
  • Continuity of care – through written records and verbal reports
  • Trust and satisfaction – patients feel cared for when they are heard and understood
  • Professional growth – reading and writing build knowledge and career

Conclusion As a health care professional, the nurse must be an attentive listener, a clear speaker, a careful reader and an accurate writer; together these LSRW roles make communication safe and effective.

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain the barriers to communication and ways to overcome them.
answer_html:
Introduction A barrier is anything that blocks, distorts or delays the message between the sender and the receiver. In hospitals, barriers can lead to misunderstanding, poor cooperation and errors.

Types of barriers

1. Physical barriers

  • Noise of machines and crowds, poor lighting, distance, closed doors, poor telephone or network connection

2. Language (semantic) barriers

  • Different languages or dialects – a Marathi-speaking patient and a Malayalam-speaking nurse
  • Medical jargon – "NPO", "ambulate", "void" confuses patients
  • Words with double meanings; poor pronunciation; wrong grammar
  • Translation errors

3. Physiological barriers

  • Pain, fatigue, fever, hearing or speech problems, poor eyesight, effects of drugs

4. Psychological (emotional) barriers

  • Fear, anxiety, anger, depression, shyness, lack of interest, preoccupation with worries

5. Socio-cultural barriers

  • Differences in age, gender, religion, education, social status and customs; hesitation of women to speak to male staff

6. Attitudinal barriers

  • Prejudice, ego, a "know-all" attitude, rudeness, not respecting others' opinions

7. Organisational barriers

  • Heavy workload, lack of time, rigid hierarchy, too many levels of communication

8. Poor listening

  • Interrupting, day-dreaming, selective listening, preparing a reply instead of listening

Ways to overcome barriers

  • Choose a quiet, private place; reduce noise
  • Use simple words in the receiver's language; avoid jargon; use an interpreter if needed
  • Speak clearly and at a moderate speed; pronounce words correctly
  • Use non-verbal cues, pictures and demonstrations
  • Relieve pain and discomfort before an important conversation
  • Show empathy and respect; be non-judgemental
  • Listen actively and ask for feedback – "Can you tell me in your own words what you will do?"
  • Respect cultural differences
  • Put important instructions in writing

Example

  • An elderly patient with poor hearing nods to everything the nurse says but takes his tablets wrongly at home. Facing him, speaking slowly and clearly, using pictures of the tablets with times, and asking him to repeat the instructions would have prevented the error.

Conclusion Communication may be blocked by physical, language, physiological, psychological, cultural, attitudinal and organisational barriers; simple language, active listening, empathy and feedback help to overcome them.

subject: Communicative English
question: Define communication. Explain the process and types of communication and the importance of communication skills for a nurse. (2 + 3 + 3 + 2)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Communication is the process of sending and receiving messages – information, ideas, thoughts and feelings – between two or more persons, through verbal and non-verbal means, so that they reach a common understanding
  • Keith Davis: communication is "the process of passing information and understanding from one person to another"
  • It is a two-way, continuous and dynamic process

(b) Process of communication (3 marks)

  1. Sender – the person who has an idea to share (the nurse)
  2. Encoding – putting the idea into words, symbols or gestures ("Please don't eat anything after 10 o'clock tonight")
  3. Message – the content to be shared
  4. Channel (medium) – the way it is sent: face-to-face talk, telephone, letter, email, chart, poster
  5. Receiver – the person who receives the message (the patient)
  6. Decoding – the receiver interprets the message
  7. Feedback – the receiver's response, which shows whether the message was understood ("So I can have tea at 9 but nothing after 10?")
  8. Noise – anything that disturbs the message (noise, pain, language difference)
  9. Context – the setting, time and relationship in which communication takes place

(c) Types of communication (3 marks)

1. According to the mode

  • Verbal – oral (talking, lectures, telephone, meetings) and written (letters, reports, notes, emails, records)
  • Non-verbal – facial expression, eye contact, gestures, posture, touch, tone, silence, personal appearance and distance (proxemics)
  • Visual – charts, graphs, posters, pictures, videos, signs

2. According to the number of people

  • Intrapersonal – with oneself (thinking)
  • Interpersonal – between two persons
  • Group – small group discussions, team meetings
  • Public / mass – lectures, radio, TV, newspapers, social media

3. According to formality

  • Formal – through official channels (circulars, reports, meetings)
  • Informal – casual, friendly conversations ("grapevine")

4. According to direction (in an organisation)

  • Downward – from seniors to juniors (instructions)
  • Upward – from juniors to seniors (reports, suggestions)
  • Horizontal (lateral) – between people at the same level (staff nurse to staff nurse)
  • Diagonal – across departments

5. According to purpose in nursing

  • Therapeutic communication – to help the patient (listening, empathy, reassurance)
  • Professional communication – with the health team (handover, reports)

Principles of effective communication (the 7 Cs)

  • Clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete and courteous
  • Suited to the receiver's level and language, given at the right time, with feedback to confirm understanding

Barriers (in brief)

  • Physical (noise, distance), language (jargon, different language), physiological (pain, hearing loss), psychological (fear, anger), cultural, attitudinal (prejudice) and organisational (workload, hierarchy)

Example from the ward

  • Poor: the nurse says quickly, "NPO after midnight, OK?" and walks away – the patient drinks tea at 6 a.m. and the surgery is postponed
  • Good: the nurse sits down and says slowly in the patient's language, "Please do not eat or drink anything, not even water or tea, after 12 o'clock tonight, because your operation is tomorrow morning. Can you tell me what you will do?" – she also places a "Nil by mouth" card on the bed

(d) Importance of communication skills for a nurse (2 marks)

  • Builds trust and a good nurse–patient relationship
  • Helps in accurate assessment and nursing history
  • Ensures patient safety – clear handover, correct understanding of orders, read-back of telephone orders
  • Makes health education effective and improves compliance
  • Reduces anxiety of patients and relatives
  • Helps teamwork and coordination with doctors and other staff
  • Supports leadership, supervision and teaching
  • Provides legal protection through clear records
  • Improves patient satisfaction and the image of the hospital

Conclusion Communication is the two-way process of sharing information and feelings through a sender, message, channel, receiver and feedback. It may be verbal, non-verbal or visual; interpersonal, group or mass; formal or informal; and it moves downward, upward and across an organisation. Good communication skills are essential for safe, caring and effective nursing practice.

subject: Communicative English
question: How should a nurse communicate with a patient who speaks a different language?
answer_html:
Introduction Patients from other states or tribal areas may not understand the nurse's language. Poor understanding can lead to fear, errors and non-cooperation.

Ways to communicate

  1. Arrange a trained interpreter or a staff member who speaks the patient's language; avoid using children as interpreters for sensitive topics
  2. Use simple words and short sentences; speak slowly and clearly, not loudly
  3. Use gestures, pictures, picture cards and demonstrations
  4. Learn a few key phrases in common local languages (e.g. Marathi, Hindi)
  5. Give written material in the patient's language
  6. Use translation apps carefully, only for simple messages
  7. Check understanding by asking the patient to repeat or show (teach-back)
  8. Be patient, respectful and aware of the patient's culture

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain digital communication in health care and its etiquette.
answer_html:
Introduction Digital (electronic) communication is the exchange of messages through electronic media – e-mail, SMS, messaging apps, phone and video calls, telemedicine, hospital information systems and social media. It is fast and convenient, but it must be used professionally and safely.

A. Uses in nursing

  • Sharing reports and information within the health team
  • Appointment reminders and follow-up messages to patients
  • Teleconsultation (e.g. the national telemedicine service e-Sanjeevani)
  • Online learning, webinars and meetings
  • Health education through videos and messages

B. Etiquette

1. E-mail

  • Write a clear subject line
  • Use a formal greeting ("Dear Sir/Madam", "Respected Ma'am") and closing ("Regards")
  • Keep the message brief, clear and polite; use correct grammar and spelling
  • Avoid SMS language and CAPITAL LETTERS (which look like shouting)
  • Attach files with clear names; mention attachments in the text
  • Sign with name and designation; reply promptly
  • Check the recipients carefully before pressing "Reply All"

2. Phone calls and messages

  • Identify yourself; speak politely; be brief
  • Avoid sending messages late at night unless urgent
  • Avoid emojis and slang in professional messages

3. Video calls and online meetings

  • Join on time; dress properly; choose a quiet, well-lit place
  • Keep the microphone muted when not speaking; look at the camera

4. Social media

  • Never post photographs or details of patients, even without names – this breaks confidentiality
  • Do not criticise patients, colleagues or the employer online
  • Keep professional boundaries – do not add patients as friends
  • Check facts before sharing health information; do not spread rumours

5. Telemedicine

  • Confirm the patient's identity, ensure privacy, obtain consent and document the consultation

C. Advantages and disadvantages

  • Advantages – speed, wide reach, saves travel and time, written record
  • Disadvantages – risk to privacy, misunderstanding (no tone of voice), information overload, distraction during work

Example – poor and good messages

  • Poor: "pls snd rpt asap" (unclear, informal)
  • Good: "Dear Sir, kindly send the blood report of Mr Suresh Wankhede (bed 7) by 4 pm today. Regards, Kavita, Staff Nurse, Ward 5."
  • The good message is complete, polite and specific – it states who, what and by when

Conclusion Digital communication helps nurses work faster and reach more people, but it requires clear, polite, professional language and strict protection of patient confidentiality.

subject: Communicative English
question: What are vowels and consonants? Give examples.
answer_html:
Introduction English has 26 letters but about 44 sounds. Sounds are divided into vowels and consonants.

Vowels

  • Sounds made with the mouth open, with no blocking of the air
  • Vowel letters: a, e, i, o, u
  • About 20 vowel sounds: 12 pure vowels (as in bit, bed, cat, cup, cook, book, car, see, saw, sir) and 8 diphthongs – two vowel sounds glided together (as in day, my, boy, go, now, ear, air, poor)

Consonants

  • Sounds made when the air is partly or fully blocked by the lips, teeth or tongue
  • 21 consonant letters (b, c, d, f, g …)
  • About 24 consonant sounds – e.g. /p/ in pain, /b/ in blood, /ʃ/ (sh) in shock, /tʃ/ (ch) in chest, /θ/ (th) in thermometer

Note: "y" can act as a vowel (rhythm) or a consonant (yes).

subject: Communicative English
question: What is word stress? Give examples.
answer_html:
Definition Word stress is the extra force (loudness, length and higher pitch) given to one syllable of a word when we say it. Wrong stress can make a word hard to understand.

Examples (stressed syllable in capitals)

  1. PA-tient
  2. HOS-pi-tal
  3. in-JEC-tion
  4. ther-MOM-e-ter
  5. med-i-CA-tion
  6. ex-am-i-NA-tion

Stress can change the meaning or part of speech

  • RE-cord (noun – a written account) / re-CORD (verb – to write down)
  • PRE-sent (noun – a gift) / pre-SENT (verb – to show)
  • OB-ject (noun) / ob-JECT (verb – to oppose)

Sentence stress: important words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives) are stressed – "Give the TABLET AFTER FOOD."

subject: Communicative English
question: What are linkers? Give examples.
answer_html:
Definition Linkers (connectives) are words or phrases that join ideas, sentences and paragraphs and show the relationship between them. They make speech and writing smooth and logical.

Types with examples

  1. Addition – and, also, moreover, in addition, furthermore
  2. Contrast – but, however, although, whereas, on the other hand
  3. Cause and effect – because, since, so, therefore, as a result
  4. Sequence – first, next, then, after that, finally
  5. Example – for example, for instance, such as
  6. Condition – if, unless, provided that
  7. Conclusion – in short, to sum up, in conclusion

Example sentence: "The patient had a high fever; therefore, the nurse started tepid sponging. However, the temperature did not fall, so she informed the doctor."

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain intonation with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction Intonation is the rise and fall of the pitch of the voice while speaking. It is the "music" of speech. The same words can carry different meanings and feelings depending on intonation. A nurse's intonation tells the patient whether she is caring, irritated, sure or unsure.

Functions of intonation

  • Shows the type of sentence – statement, question or command
  • Expresses feelings and attitudes – politeness, surprise, anger, doubt, concern
  • Shows which word is important
  • Marks the end of an idea or that the speaker has more to say

Patterns of intonation

1. Falling intonation (↘) – the voice falls at the end

  • Statements: "Your operation is tomorrow ↘."
  • Wh-questions (what, where, when, why, how): "Where is the pain ↘?"
  • Commands and instructions: "Take a deep breath ↘."
  • Shows certainty and completeness

2. Rising intonation (↗) – the voice rises at the end

  • Yes/no questions: "Are you feeling better ↗?" "Did you sleep well ↗?"
  • Polite requests: "Could you sit up, please ↗?"
  • Showing doubt, surprise or interest: "You walked all the way here ↗?"
  • In lists, every item except the last: "Bring your file ↗, reports ↗ and medicines ↘."

3. Fall–rise intonation (↘↗)

  • Shows uncertainty, polite disagreement or a hint that something more is meant: "The report is normal… but we need one more test ↘↗."

4. Rise–fall intonation (↗↘)

  • Shows strong feeling – surprise, approval or sarcasm: "Oh, that's wonderful ↗↘!"

Common errors of Indian learners

  • Using a flat (monotonous) tone that sounds rude or uninterested
  • Using falling intonation for yes/no questions, which sounds like an order

Tips for practice

  • Listen to news readers and good speakers; record and listen to your own voice; read dialogues aloud; mark arrows on sentences before reading

Nursing importance

  • A warm, rising, polite tone makes requests acceptable; a calm, steady tone reassures anxious patients; a firm falling tone is used for important instructions

Conclusion Intonation – falling, rising, fall–rise and rise–fall – adds meaning and feeling to words; correct intonation makes the nurse's speech clear, polite and reassuring.

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain the LSRGW skills and their importance for nurses.
answer_html:
Introduction LSRGW stands for Listening, Speaking, Reading, Grammar and Writing – the basic skills of a language. In nursing, English is used for textbooks, records, reports, drug labels, examinations and communication with doctors and patients from different states. Developing these skills improves both professional work and confidence.

1. Listening (L)

  • The first skill a child learns; receiving and understanding spoken messages
  • Types: active, passive, critical, empathetic and appreciative listening
  • For nurses: understanding patients' complaints, doctors' orders, handover reports, lectures and announcements

2. Speaking (S)

  • Expressing ideas clearly with correct pronunciation (vowels and consonants), word and sentence stress and intonation
  • For nurses: explaining procedures, health teaching, reporting to doctors, telephone talks, presentations

3. Reading (R)

  • Understanding written text – skimming, scanning, intensive and extensive reading
  • Building medical vocabulary – prefixes, suffixes, root words (gastr- = stomach, -itis = inflammation, so gastritis = inflammation of the stomach)
  • For nurses: case sheets, prescriptions, drug labels, journals, policies

4. Grammar (G)

  • The rules of a language – parts of speech, tenses, subject–verb agreement, articles, prepositions, linkers
  • For nurses: correct tenses in records ("The patient was given paracetamol 500 mg at 10 a.m."), clear sentences that cannot be misread

5. Writing (W)

  • Writing simple sentences and short paragraphs, notes, letters, reports and records
  • For nurses: nursing notes, care plans, incident reports, applications, patient instructions

Interrelationship

  • Listening and reading are receptive skills; speaking and writing are productive skills; grammar supports all of them
  • Good listening improves speaking; good reading improves writing

Importance for nurses

  • Patient safety – correct understanding and recording of orders
  • Professional communication with the health team
  • Academic success – textbooks, exams and presentations are in English
  • Career growth – interviews, jobs in other states and abroad (e.g. IELTS, OET)
  • Confidence in dealing with people

Conclusion Listening, speaking, reading, grammar and writing are interlinked language skills; mastering them helps nurses communicate safely, learn effectively and grow professionally.

subject: Communicative English
question: What is a tense? Explain the types of tenses with their structure and examples.
answer_html:
Definition

  • A tense is the form of a verb that shows the time of an action – present, past or future – and whether the action is simple, continuing or completed
  • There are 3 main tenses, each with 4 forms (aspects) – simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous – making 12 tenses in all

Verb forms used: V1 (base – give), V2 (past – gave), V3 (past participle – given), V-ing (giving).

A. Present tense

1. Simple present – Subject + V1 (+ s/es for he, she, it)

  • Uses: habits, routines, general truths, schedules
  • "The nurse checks the BP every morning." "The heart pumps blood." "The OPD opens at 9 a.m."
  • Negative: "He does not smoke." Question: "Do you have pain?"

2. Present continuous – Subject + am/is/are + V-ing

  • Uses: actions happening now; temporary actions; planned future
  • "The patient is sleeping now." "We are attending a workshop this week."

3. Present perfect – Subject + has/have + V3

  • Uses: completed actions connected with the present; experiences; recent actions (with just, already, yet, ever, never)
  • "The doctor has seen the report." "I have never assisted in a caesarean section."

4. Present perfect continuous – Subject + has/have been + V-ing (+ since / for)

  • Uses: an action that started in the past and is still continuing
  • "The patient has been coughing for two days." "She has been working here since 2019."
  • Common error: "He is having fever since two days" ✗ → "He has been having fever for two days" ✓

B. Past tense

5. Simple past – Subject + V2

  • Uses: actions completed at a definite time in the past
  • "The patient was admitted yesterday." "I gave the injection at 8 a.m."

6. Past continuous – Subject + was/were + V-ing

  • Uses: an action in progress at a time in the past; often interrupted by another action
  • "The patient was sleeping when the doctor came."

7. Past perfect – Subject + had + V3

  • Uses: an action completed before another past action
  • "The patient had taken breakfast before the sample was collected."

8. Past perfect continuous – Subject + had been + V-ing

  • Uses: an action that continued for some time before another past action
  • "He had been vomiting for six hours before he was brought to the hospital."

C. Future tense

9. Simple future – Subject + will/shall + V1

  • Uses: future actions, promises, predictions, decisions
  • "The surgeon will operate tomorrow." "I will bring your medicines."

10. Future continuous – Subject + will be + V-ing

  • Uses: an action that will be in progress at a future time
  • "At 9 a.m. tomorrow, the students will be attending the clinical class."

11. Future perfect – Subject + will have + V3

  • Uses: an action that will be completed before a certain future time
  • "By 5 p.m., the IV fluid will have finished."

12. Future perfect continuous – Subject + will have been + V-ing

  • Uses: the duration of an action up to a future time
  • "By next June, she will have been working in this hospital for ten years."

Summary table (verb: give)

Time Simple Continuous Perfect Perfect continuous
Present I give I am giving I have given I have been giving
Past I gave I was giving I had given I had been giving
Future I will give I will be giving I will have given I will have been giving

Tenses in nursing records

  • Simple past and passive voice are mostly used: "Inj. ceftriaxone 1 g IV was given at 10 a.m." "The patient complained of headache."
  • Never write in the future tense in records ("will be given") – record only what has been done

Common errors

  • "I am knowing him" ✗ → "I know him" ✓ (stative verbs such as know, like, believe are not used in the continuous form)
  • "He did not came" ✗ → "He did not come" ✓
  • "She has came" ✗ → "She has come" ✓
  • "Yesterday I have seen him" ✗ → "Yesterday I saw him" ✓

Conclusion Tense shows the time of an action. The present, past and future tenses each have simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous forms, making twelve tenses with clear structures; using the correct tense makes speech and nursing records accurate and clear.

subject: Communicative English
question: What are articles? Give the rules for using a, an and the.
answer_html:
Definition Articles are words used before nouns to show whether the noun is indefinite (a, an) or definite (the).

Rules

  1. "A" – before words beginning with a consonant sound: a patient, a bed, a uniform ("yoo" sound), a one-day course
  2. "An" – before words beginning with a vowel sound: an injection, an operation, an hour (silent h), an MRI, an X-ray
  3. "The" – before something specific or already mentioned: "I gave the tablet you prescribed."
    • before unique things: the sun, the earth
    • with superlatives: the best nurse
    • with names of rivers, seas and some organisations: the Ganga, the WHO
  4. No article – before names of people, languages, subjects and meals in general: "She studies anatomy." "Breakfast is served at 8 am."

subject: Communicative English
question: What is sentence stress? Give examples.
answer_html:
Definition Sentence stress is giving extra force (loudness, length and pitch) to the important words in a sentence, while other words are spoken quickly and lightly.

Rules

  • Content words are usually stressed – nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs, negatives and question words
  • Function words are usually unstressed – articles, prepositions, pronouns, helping verbs and conjunctions

Examples (stressed words in capitals)

  • "The DOCTOR will SEE you NOW."
  • "TAKE this TABLET after FOOD."
  • "WHERE does it HURT?"

Contrastive stress changes the meaning

  • "I gave HIM the medicine" – him, not someone else
  • "I GAVE him the medicine" – I did give it

Importance: makes speech clear and natural and highlights key instructions for patients.

subject: Communicative English
question: What are homophones and commonly confused words? Give examples from nursing.
answer_html:
Definition Homophones are words that sound alike but differ in meaning and spelling. Many medical words also look or sound similar, and confusing them can cause serious errors.

Examples

  1. Ileum (part of the small intestine) – ilium (hip bone)
  2. Dysphagia (difficulty in swallowing) – dysphasia (difficulty in speaking)
  3. Perineal (of the perineum) – peroneal (of the outer leg)
  4. Prostate (a gland) – prostrate (lying face down)
  5. Hypo- (below normal) – hyper- (above normal)
  6. Affect (verb – to influence) – effect (noun – result)
  7. Advice (noun) – advise (verb)
  8. Principal (head of a college) – principle (rule)
  9. Lose (to misplace) – loose (not tight)
  10. Compliment (praise) – complement (complete)

Nursing: spell and pronounce clearly; read back orders to avoid mistakes.

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain active and passive voice with rules and examples.
answer_html:
Introduction Voice shows whether the subject does the action (active voice) or receives the action (passive voice).

  • Active: The nurse gave the injection.
  • Passive: The injection was given by the nurse.

A. Rules for changing active into passive

  1. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive sentence
  2. Use the correct form of "be" (according to the tense) + the past participle (V3) of the main verb
  3. The subject of the active sentence comes after "by" – it is often left out when it is unknown or unimportant ("The patient was shifted to the ICU.")
  4. Pronouns change: I → me, we → us, he → him, she → her, they → them
  5. Only transitive verbs (verbs with an object) can be changed into passive voice

B. Voice in different tenses

Tense Active Passive
Simple present The nurse checks the BP. The BP is checked by the nurse.
Present continuous The nurse is checking the BP. The BP is being checked by the nurse.
Present perfect The nurse has checked the BP. The BP has been checked by the nurse.
Simple past The nurse checked the BP. The BP was checked by the nurse.
Past continuous The nurse was checking the BP. The BP was being checked by the nurse.
Simple future The nurse will check the BP. The BP will be checked by the nurse.
Modal verbs The nurse must check the BP. The BP must be checked by the nurse.

C. Special forms

  • Questions: "Did the doctor see the patient?" → "Was the patient seen by the doctor?"
  • Imperatives (commands): "Close the door." → "Let the door be closed." or "You are requested to close the door."

D. Use in nursing

  • Passive voice is common in reports and documentation, where the action matters more than the doer: "The patient was admitted at 10 am. IV fluids were started."
  • Active voice is clearer and more direct for instructions to patients: "Take this tablet after food."

E. Practice (with answers)

  1. The doctor examined the patient. → The patient was examined by the doctor.
  2. The sister is preparing the tray. → The tray is being prepared by the sister.
  3. They will discharge him tomorrow. → He will be discharged tomorrow.
  4. The ward boy has cleaned the ward. → The ward has been cleaned by the ward boy.
  5. We must record the vital signs. → The vital signs must be recorded.

Conclusion In active voice the subject acts, and in passive voice the subject receives the action; passive voice is formed with "be" + past participle and is widely used in nursing reports, while active voice suits instructions.

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain the parts of speech with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction Words in English are classified into eight parts of speech according to the work they do in a sentence.

1. Noun – the name of a person, place, thing or idea

  • Examples: nurse, Nagpur, thermometer, health, kindness
  • Kinds: proper (Florence), common (patient), collective (team), abstract (honesty), material (cotton); countable (bed) and uncountable (water)

2. Pronoun – a word used instead of a noun

  • Examples: he, she, it, they, who, this, myself
  • "The patient is tired. He wants to sleep."

3. Verb – shows an action or state

  • Examples: give, check, walk, is, feel
  • Main verbs (give) and helping verbs (is, has, do, will, can)
  • "The nurse checks the pulse."

4. Adjective – describes a noun or pronoun

  • Examples: high fever, clean bed, three tablets, anxious patient

5. Adverb – describes a verb, adjective or another adverb (how, when, where, how much)

  • Examples: slowly, gently, immediately, very, here
  • "Remove the dressing gently."

6. Preposition – shows the relation of a noun or pronoun to another word

  • Examples: in, on, at, under, with, after
  • "Keep the tray on the trolley."

7. Conjunction – joins words or sentences

  • Examples: and, but, or, because, although, when
  • "He has fever and cough." "She is tired but happy."

8. Interjection – expresses sudden feeling

  • Examples: Oh! Ouch! Alas! Hurray! Wow!

Example sentence analysed "Oh! The tired nurse quickly gave him a warm drink because he was shivering."

  • Oh – interjection; tired, warm – adjectives; nurse, drink – nouns; quickly – adverb; gave, was shivering – verbs; him, he – pronouns; because – conjunction

Note: the part of speech depends on how the word is used:

  • "Her dress is white." (noun) – "Dress the wound." (verb)
  • "He works hard." (adverb) – "It is a hard bed." (adjective)

Determiners (a related group)

  • Words placed before nouns to make their meaning clear – articles (a, an, the), demonstratives (this, that), possessives (my, his), quantifiers (some, many, few) and numbers
  • "This patient needs two pillows."

Conclusion The eight parts of speech – noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction and interjection – are the building blocks of sentences; knowing them helps nurses speak and write correct English.

subject: Communicative English
question: Write a paragraph of about 150 words on "The importance of hand washing".
answer_html:
How to write a good paragraph

  • Topic sentence – the first sentence states the main idea
  • Supporting sentences – give reasons, facts and examples
  • Concluding sentence – sums up or gives a message
  • Unity – every sentence is about one idea
  • Coherence – sentences follow a logical order, joined by linkers (first, moreover, for example, therefore, finally)
  • Use simple, correct sentences and avoid repetition

Model paragraph

The Importance of Hand Washing

Hand washing is the simplest and most effective way to prevent the spread of infection. Our hands touch many surfaces every day and carry germs that cannot be seen. When we touch our eyes, nose, mouth or food, these germs enter the body and cause diseases such as diarrhoea, typhoid, influenza and COVID-19. In hospitals, the hands of health workers are the main route by which infections pass from one patient to another. Therefore, nurses must clean their hands before and after touching every patient and after handling body fluids. Washing with soap and water for at least forty to sixty seconds, or using an alcohol-based hand rub, removes most germs. Children should be taught to wash their hands before eating and after using the toilet. Thus, a habit that takes less than a minute can save many lives.

Features shown in the model

  • The first sentence is the topic sentence
  • Linkers such as therefore and thus connect ideas
  • Facts and examples support the main idea
  • The last sentence concludes with a strong message

Types of paragraphs

  • Descriptive – describes a person, place or thing (a hospital ward)
  • Narrative – tells a story or event in time order (my first day in the hospital)
  • Expository – explains or gives information (the importance of hand washing)
  • Persuasive – tries to convince the reader (why everyone should donate blood)

Common mistakes to avoid

  • No clear topic sentence; mixing several ideas
  • Very long sentences or repeated words
  • Missing linkers, so the ideas seem disconnected
  • Spelling and punctuation errors

subject: Communicative English
question: What is a sentence? Explain the types of sentences with examples. (2 + 4 + 4)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • A sentence is a group of words that makes complete sense
  • It begins with a capital letter and ends with a full stop (.), question mark (?) or exclamation mark (!)
  • It has two parts:
    • Subject – the person or thing we are talking about
    • Predicate – what we say about the subject; it contains the verb
  • Example: "The patient | is sleeping." (subject | predicate)
  • A clause is a group of words with a subject and a verb; an independent clause makes complete sense by itself, while a dependent (subordinate) clause does not

(b) Types of sentences according to function (4 marks)

1. Declarative (assertive) sentence – makes a statement

  • Affirmative: "The patient is stable."
  • Negative: "He does not smoke."

2. Interrogative sentence – asks a question

  • Yes/No questions: "Have you taken your medicine?"
  • Wh- questions: "Where is the pain?" "When did the fever start?"

3. Imperative sentence – gives a command, request, advice or instruction

  • "Take a deep breath." "Please sign here." "Do not eat anything after midnight."

4. Exclamatory sentence – expresses strong feeling

  • "What a quick recovery!" "How painful it is!"

5. Optative sentence – expresses a wish or prayer

  • "May you get well soon!"

(c) Types of sentences according to structure (4 marks)

1. Simple sentence – one independent clause (one subject and one finite verb)

  • "The doctor examined the patient."
  • "The nurse checked the drip."

2. Compound sentence – two or more independent clauses joined by coordinating conjunctions – for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so (FANBOYS)

  • "The patient was in pain, so the nurse gave him an analgesic."
  • "She wanted to go home, but the doctor advised rest."

3. Complex sentence – one independent clause and one or more dependent clauses, joined by subordinating conjunctions or relative pronouns (because, when, although, if, since, who, which, that)

  • "When the doctor arrived, the nurse gave the report."
  • "The patient who was admitted yesterday has been shifted to the ward."

4. Compound–complex sentence – two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause

  • "Although she was tired, the nurse stayed late, and she completed the report."

Transformation – the same idea in three structures

  • Simple: "Being tired, the nurse sat down."
  • Compound: "The nurse was tired, so she sat down."
  • Complex: "The nurse sat down because she was tired."

Common errors

  • Sentence fragment – an incomplete sentence: "Because the patient was in pain." (needs a main clause)
  • Run-on sentence – two sentences joined without punctuation: "The patient is stable he can go home." → "The patient is stable, so he can go home."

Importance for nurses

  • Use short, clear, complete sentences in documentation
  • Use imperative sentences for patient instructions
  • Use interrogative sentences in history-taking
  • Varied sentence structures make reports and presentations clear and interesting

Basic sentence patterns

Pattern Example
Subject + Verb The patient slept.
Subject + Verb + Object The nurse gave the tablet.
Subject + Verb + Complement The child is feverish.
Subject + Verb + Indirect object + Direct object The doctor gave the patient a prescription.
Subject + Verb + Object + Complement The news made the family happy.

Changing the type of sentence (same meaning)

  • Declarative → interrogative: "The report is ready." → "Is the report ready?"
  • Declarative → exclamatory: "It is a very beautiful garden." → "What a beautiful garden it is!"
  • Declarative → imperative: "You should rest." → "Rest."

Phrase and clause

  • A phrase has no subject–verb pair: "in the morning", "after the operation"
  • A clause has a subject and a verb: "after the patient woke up"

Sentences in nursing notes

  • Nursing notes often use short phrases for speed, but each entry must still be clear and unambiguous
  • Write: "Patient complained of chest pain at 10.30 pm. ECG taken. Dr Joshi informed at 10.35 pm."
  • Avoid vague sentences such as "Patient OK" – state what was observed: "Patient resting, pulse 82/min, no complaints."
  • Use the past tense for events and the time for every action

Conclusion A sentence is a group of words that makes complete sense; by function, sentences are declarative, interrogative, imperative, exclamatory or optative, and by structure, simple, compound, complex or compound–complex.

subject: Communicative English
question: Differentiate between hearing and listening.
answer_html:
Introduction Hearing and listening are often used as the same word, but they are different.

Hearing Listening
a physical process – sound waves reach the ear a mental, active process – attending to, understanding and responding to sounds
automatic and passive voluntary and needs concentration
needs only normal ears needs attention, interest and effort
we hear many sounds at once (traffic, fan, voices) we listen to selected sounds with meaning
example: hearing noise in the ward example: listening carefully to a patient describe his pain

Saying: "We hear with our ears, but we listen with our minds."

subject: Communicative English
question: Mention the types of listening.
answer_html:
Introduction People listen in different ways depending on the purpose.

Types of listening

  1. Discriminative listening – recognising differences in sounds and tone (noticing wheezing, a change in the patient's voice)
  2. Comprehensive (informational) listening – to understand information (lectures, instructions)
  3. Critical (evaluative) listening – judging whether a message is true and logical (advertisements, arguments)
  4. Empathetic (therapeutic) listening – understanding the speaker's feelings (listening to an anxious patient)
  5. Appreciative listening – for enjoyment (music, poetry)
  6. Active listening – full attention with feedback (nodding, paraphrasing)
  7. Passive listening – listening without responding
  8. Selective listening – hearing only what one wants to hear (a barrier)

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain the barriers to effective listening and the ways to overcome them.
answer_html:
Introduction Listening is the active process of receiving, understanding, remembering and responding to spoken messages. Studies show that people remember only a small part of what they hear. In hospitals, poor listening can lead to wrong doses, missed symptoms and unhappy patients.

A. Barriers to effective listening

1. Physical (environmental) barriers

  • Noise of machines, alarms, telephones, crowded wards, poor acoustics, uncomfortable seating, distance from the speaker

2. Physiological barriers

  • Hearing problems, fatigue after night duty, hunger, illness, headache

3. Psychological barriers

  • Pre-occupation with one's own worries; day-dreaming; anxiety; anger; lack of interest
  • Prejudice against the speaker or the topic ("This patient always complains")
  • Closed mind – thinking one already knows

4. Language barriers

  • Unfamiliar accent, dialect, fast speech, technical words, poor vocabulary of the listener

5. Speaker-related barriers

  • Speaking too fast, too softly or in a monotonous tone; unclear ideas

6. Bad listening habits

  • Interrupting the speaker
  • Preparing a reply instead of listening
  • Selective listening – hearing only what one likes
  • Pseudo-listening – pretending to listen
  • Information overload – too much information at once
  • Multitasking – using the mobile phone while listening

B. Ways to overcome barriers (to improve listening)

  1. Remove distractions – find a quiet place, switch off or silence the mobile phone
  2. Pay full attention – face the speaker, maintain eye contact, lean slightly forward
  3. Keep an open mind; avoid prejudging the speaker
  4. Do not interrupt; let the speaker finish
  5. Listen for main ideas and key words; take notes during lectures and handover
  6. Ask questions to clarify – "Do you mean…?"
  7. Paraphrase and summarise – "So the pain started after lunch and spreads to your back?"
  8. Observe non-verbal cues – facial expression, tone, posture
  9. Show interest with nods and short responses ("I see", "Go on")
  10. Control emotions – listen first, react later
  11. Improve vocabulary and get used to different accents by listening to English news and talks
  12. Take care of health – adequate rest; get hearing checked

Conclusion Listening may be blocked by noise, fatigue, preoccupation, prejudice, language problems and bad habits; removing distractions, paying full attention, keeping an open mind, not interrupting, asking questions and paraphrasing make listening effective.

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain how to listen effectively to lectures and presentations.
answer_html:
Introduction Much of a nursing student's learning comes from lectures, demonstrations, seminars and presentations. Listening attentively to them, and making good notes, improves understanding, memory and examination performance.

A. Before the lecture

  1. Prepare – read the topic briefly in the textbook; revise the previous class
  2. Sit in front, where you can see and hear clearly
  3. Keep a notebook and pen ready; switch off or silence the mobile phone
  4. Be rested and fed – hunger and tiredness reduce attention

B. During the lecture

  1. Listen for the structure – the introduction, main points and conclusion
  2. Notice signal words – "first", "the most important point is", "for example", "in conclusion", "remember that" – they show key ideas
  3. Listen for main ideas, not every word
  4. Take notes – key words, short phrases, abbreviations, diagrams and flow charts (do not try to write everything)
  5. Watch the speaker's non-verbal cues – pauses, emphasis, gestures and what is written on the board or slides
  6. Ask questions at the proper time if something is not clear
  7. Avoid distractions – talking with friends, day-dreaming, mobile phones
  8. Listen critically – think about how the information applies in the ward

C. After the lecture

  1. Review and complete your notes the same day – add missing points from the textbook
  2. Summarise the lecture in a few lines
  3. Discuss with classmates; clarify doubts with the teacher
  4. Revise regularly

D. Listening to presentations and seminars

  • Note the speaker's purpose and main message
  • Evaluate the evidence and examples given
  • Prepare questions for the discussion time
  • Give polite, constructive feedback

Reproducing verbatim

  • In some activities (dictation, telephone orders, instructions), the listener must reproduce exactly what was said – listen carefully, write immediately and read it back to confirm

Conclusion Effective listening to lectures needs preparation, attention to structure and signal words, good note taking, questions and review after class; these habits greatly improve learning.

subject: Communicative English
question: Define listening. Explain the process of listening, the types of listening and the ways to improve listening skills. (2 + 3 + 3 + 2)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Listening is the active process of receiving, attending to, understanding, remembering and responding to spoken and non-verbal messages
  • Hearing is only the physical reception of sound; listening needs attention and effort
  • Listening is the first language skill we learn and the one we use most – a large part of our communication time is spent listening
  • Attentive listening means giving full, focused attention to the speaker

(b) Process (stages) of listening – the HURIER model (3 marks)

  1. Hearing (receiving) – the sound waves reach the ear; the listener picks out the message from background noise
  2. Understanding – the listener interprets the words and the language, using vocabulary and knowledge
  3. Remembering – the message is stored in memory for later use (taking notes helps)
  4. Interpreting – the listener understands the feelings and intentions behind the words, using tone and body language
  5. Evaluating – judging the message: is it true, logical, complete? Separating facts from opinions
  6. Responding – giving feedback – verbal ("I understand") or non-verbal (nodding), or acting on the message

Example: a patient says, "I'm fine, sister," in a low voice, avoiding eye contact. The nurse hears the words, understands them, remembers that he refused lunch, interprets his sad tone, evaluates that he may not be fine, and responds: "You seem a little low today. Would you like to talk?"

(c) Types of listening (3 marks)

  1. Discriminative listening – distinguishing sounds and changes in tone (a nurse notices a change in a child's cry)
  2. Comprehensive (informational) listening – understanding information and instructions (lectures, doctors' orders, handover)
  3. Critical (evaluative) listening – analysing and judging a message before accepting it (sales talk, health claims on TV)
  4. Empathetic (therapeutic) listening – understanding the speaker's feelings and point of view; very important in nursing (listening to a grieving mother)
  5. Appreciative listening – listening for enjoyment (music, poetry, a good speech)
  6. Active listening – full attention with verbal and non-verbal feedback, paraphrasing and clarifying
  7. Passive listening – listening without responding (radio in the background)
  8. Selective listening – hearing only what one wants to hear; a barrier

Listening to different texts

  • Announcements – listen for key details: time, place, number, change
  • Instructions and demonstrations – listen for the sequence of steps; ask for repetition if needed
  • Narratives and descriptions – listen for who, what, when, where, why and how
  • Discussions – listen to different viewpoints before giving your own

Barriers to effective listening (in brief)

  • Physical – noise, alarms, poor acoustics, distance
  • Physiological – hearing problems, fatigue after night duty, hunger
  • Psychological – preoccupation, day-dreaming, anxiety, prejudice, a closed mind
  • Language – unfamiliar accent, fast speech, technical terms
  • Bad habits – interrupting, preparing a reply, pseudo-listening, using the mobile phone

Signal words that help the listener

  • Sequence: first, next, then, finally
  • Importance: the main point is, remember that, note that
  • Example: for example, such as
  • Contrast: but, however, on the other hand
  • Conclusion: to sum up, in short

(d) Ways to improve listening skills (2 marks)

  1. Prepare – be rested, interested and free from distractions; silence the phone
  2. Pay attention – face the speaker, maintain eye contact
  3. Keep an open mind; avoid prejudices
  4. Do not interrupt; wait for the speaker to finish
  5. Listen for main ideas and signal words
  6. Take brief notes
  7. Ask clarifying questions and paraphrase to check understanding
  8. Observe non-verbal cues
  9. Show interest with nods and short verbal responses
  10. Practise – listen to English news, podcasts and lectures; do dictation exercises

Importance of attentive listening in nursing

  • Accurate assessment and history
  • Patient safety – correct understanding of orders and read-back of telephone orders
  • Emotional support – patients feel valued and understood
  • Better teamwork and fewer misunderstandings

Conclusion Listening is an active process of hearing, understanding, remembering, interpreting, evaluating and responding. There are many types – discriminative, comprehensive, critical, empathetic, appreciative, active and passive. By removing distractions, paying full attention, keeping an open mind, asking questions and practising regularly, nurses can become attentive listeners who give safer and more caring care.

subject: Communicative English
question: What is verbatim reproduction? Why is it important for nurses?
answer_html:
Definition Verbatim reproduction means repeating or writing down a message in exactly the same words in which it was heard, without changing, adding or leaving out anything.

Importance for nurses

  1. Verbal and telephone orders – the drug name, dose, route and time must be written and read back exactly
  2. Critical laboratory values reported on the phone
  3. Patient's own words in the history – e.g. Patient states: "I feel as if someone is sitting on my chest."
  4. Medico-legal statements and records
  5. Instructions from seniors and doctors

How to do it

  • Listen attentively; write immediately
  • Use quotation marks for the exact words
  • Read back and confirm with the speaker

subject: Communicative English
question: Differentiate between formal and informal conversation with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction The way we speak changes with the person and the situation.

Formal conversation Informal conversation
with seniors, doctors, officials, strangers, patients with friends, family, close colleagues
polite, complete sentences, correct grammar casual, short forms, slang
titles used – "Sir", "Madam", "Dr. Patil" first names, nicknames
no short forms – "I would like to…" short forms – "I'd", "gonna", "OK"
example: "Good morning, Sir. May I report the condition of the patient in bed 12?" example: "Hey Priya, are you coming for lunch?"

Neutral conversation – polite but relaxed, used with colleagues and patients in daily work: "Good morning, Mr. Rao. How are you feeling today?"

subject: Communicative English
question: List the points of telephone etiquette.
answer_html:
Introduction Telephone etiquette means polite and professional behaviour while using the telephone. In hospitals, telephone calls often carry urgent information.

Points of telephone etiquette

  1. Answer promptly – within three rings
  2. Greet and identify yourself and the ward – "Good morning, Ward 5, Staff Nurse Meena speaking"
  3. Speak clearly, politely and at a moderate speed; smile while speaking
  4. Listen carefully; do not interrupt
  5. Keep a pen and paper ready; note down messages – name, number, time, message
  6. Read back telephone orders and important numbers to confirm
  7. Keep calls short and to the point; avoid personal calls on duty
  8. Do not leave the caller waiting long on hold
  9. Maintain confidentiality – do not give patient information to unknown callers
  10. End politely – "Thank you, Sir. I will inform the sister in charge."

subject: Communicative English
question: Give phrases used for making requests and asking permission.
answer_html:
Introduction Polite phrases make requests and permissions acceptable and respectful.

Making requests

  1. "Could you please sit up for a moment?"
  2. "Would you mind opening your mouth?"
  3. "Can you please pass me the BP apparatus?"
  4. "I would be grateful if you could sign this form."

Asking permission

  1. "May I take your temperature?"
  2. "Could I examine your abdomen, please?"
  3. "Is it all right if I draw the curtains?"
  4. "Do you mind if I check your dressing?"

Responses

  • Agreeing: "Sure.", "Yes, of course.", "Please go ahead."
  • Refusing politely: "I'm sorry, but visitors are not allowed in the ICU now. You may visit at 5 p.m."

subject: Communicative English
question: Write a dialogue between a nurse and a newly admitted patient.
answer_html:
Situation: Mr. Ramesh Kale, 52 years, is admitted to the medical ward with fever and cough. Staff Nurse Sneha receives him.

Dialogue

Nurse: Good afternoon, Sir. I am Sneha, the staff nurse of this ward. May I know your name, please?

Patient: Good afternoon, Sister. I am Ramesh Kale.

Nurse: Welcome, Mr. Kale. Please sit on this bed. Are you comfortable?

Patient: Yes, thank you. But I am feeling very weak.

Nurse: I understand. You have fever and cough, don't you? How long have you had these problems?

Patient: For the last four days, Sister. The cough is worse at night.

Nurse: I see. Do you have any difficulty in breathing or chest pain?

Patient: A little chest pain when I cough.

Nurse: All right. I will check your temperature, pulse and blood pressure now. May I put this thermometer under your arm?

Patient: Yes, please.

Nurse: Your temperature is 101 °F. Don't worry; the doctor will see you shortly, and we will give you medicine for the fever. Are you allergic to any medicine?

Patient: No, Sister, not that I know of.

Nurse: Good. Let me show you around. This is your locker for your belongings. The toilet is on the right side of the corridor. If you need help, please press this call bell, and a nurse will come.

Patient: Thank you. When can my wife visit me?

Nurse: Visiting hours are from 4 to 7 in the evening. One relative can stay with you at night. Please keep your valuables with your wife.

Patient: Okay. Will I need any tests?

Nurse: Yes, the doctor may advise a blood test and a chest X-ray. I will explain each test before it is done.

Patient: Thank you, Sister. I feel better now.

Nurse: You're welcome, Mr. Kale. Please take rest. I will come back in a few minutes with a glass of water and to complete your file.

Points shown in the dialogue

  • Greeting and introduction, using the patient's name
  • Open and closed questions for the history
  • Asking permission before a procedure
  • Reassurance and empathy
  • Orientation to the ward, call bell and visiting hours
  • Polite, simple language and a warm closing

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain the factors influencing speech and the qualities of effective speaking.
answer_html:
Introduction Speaking is the productive skill of expressing ideas, information and feelings in words. A nurse speaks constantly – to patients, relatives, doctors and students. How well she speaks depends on many factors.

A. Factors influencing speech

1. Physical factors

  • Health of the speech organs – lips, teeth, tongue, palate, vocal cords; breathing; hearing
  • Fatigue, sore throat, dental problems

2. Psychological factors

  • Confidence, anxiety, stage fear, shyness, mood, attitude towards the listener
  • Fear of making mistakes in English

3. Knowledge and preparation

  • Knowledge of the subject; vocabulary; grammar; preparation

4. Mother tongue influence (MTI)

  • Regional accent, wrong stress and pronunciation – e.g. confusion between "v" and "w", or adding sounds ("iskool" for "school")

5. Environment

  • Noise, size of the audience, formal or informal setting, distance

6. Relationship with the listener

  • Speech changes with age, status and familiarity of the listener – formal with doctors, gentle with patients

7. Culture

  • Norms about politeness, eye contact, loudness and topics to avoid

8. Purpose of speech

  • Informing, instructing, persuading, comforting or entertaining

B. Qualities of effective speaking

  1. Clarity – clear pronunciation and simple words
  2. Correct grammar and vocabulary
  3. Proper stress and intonation – not monotonous
  4. Suitable speed, volume and pauses – neither too fast nor too loud
  5. Confidence – steady voice, good posture, eye contact
  6. Politeness and courtesy – "please", "thank you", "sorry"
  7. Brevity – to the point
  8. Logical order – beginning, middle and end
  9. Matching body language – facial expression and gestures that support the words
  10. Audience awareness – adapting language to the listener (simple words for patients, technical terms for doctors)
  11. Listening and feedback – speaking is a two-way process

Tips for improvement

  • Read aloud daily, record and listen to yourself, practise with friends, learn correct pronunciation from dictionaries and news readers, and take part in seminars and role plays

Conclusion Speech is influenced by physical, psychological, linguistic, environmental and cultural factors; clear, correct, confident, polite and well-organised speaking makes a nurse an effective communicator.

subject: Communicative English
question: Write a telephone conversation in which a staff nurse reports a patient's condition to the doctor.
answer_html:
Situation: At 2 a.m., Mrs. Shobha Rane (bed 8, post-operative day 1 after abdominal hysterectomy) has a fall in BP. Staff Nurse Anita telephones the duty doctor, Dr. Deshmukh, using the SBAR format.

Conversation

Doctor: Hello, Dr. Deshmukh speaking.

Nurse: Good morning, Doctor. This is Staff Nurse Anita from the Gynaecology Ward. I am calling about Mrs. Shobha Rane in bed 8.

Doctor: Yes, Sister. What is the problem?

Nurse (Situation): Doctor, her blood pressure has dropped to 90/60 mmHg, and her pulse is 112 per minute. She is complaining of giddiness.

Doctor: I see. Tell me about her.

Nurse (Background): She is 45 years old and had an abdominal hysterectomy yesterday at 11 a.m. Her BP was 120/80 mmHg at 10 p.m. She is on IV Ringer's lactate at 100 ml per hour.

Doctor: What else have you noticed?

Nurse (Assessment): Her dressing is dry, but the drain has collected 250 ml of blood in the last two hours. Urine output in the last two hours is only 40 ml. She looks pale and her skin is cold and clammy. I am worried that she may be bleeding.

Doctor: Right. What have you done so far?

Nurse (Recommendation): I have raised the foot end of the bed and started oxygen at 4 litres per minute. Could you please come and see her immediately? Should I send a sample for haemoglobin and cross-matching?

Doctor: Yes, Sister. Increase the IV fluid to run fast, send blood for haemoglobin and grouping and cross-matching, and keep two units of blood reserved. I am coming in five minutes.

Nurse: Thank you, Doctor. Let me read back the orders: run the IV fluid fast, send blood for haemoglobin and grouping and cross-matching, and reserve two units of blood. You are coming in five minutes.

Doctor: Correct.

Nurse: Thank you, Doctor. I will check her vitals every 15 minutes until you arrive.

Points shown

  • Identification of self, ward and patient
  • SBAR – Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation – clear and brief
  • Use of exact figures
  • Read-back of telephone orders to avoid errors
  • Polite, formal language and a clear closing
  • The orders are then documented with time and countersigned by the doctor as per policy

subject: Communicative English
question: Write a conversation showing how a nurse handles a complaint from a patient's relative.
answer_html:
Situation: Mr. Sunil Patil, the son of a patient in bed 15, comes to the nurses' station angry that his father's dressing has not been changed since morning.

Conversation

Relative: Sister, this is too much! My father's dressing has not been changed since morning. Nobody cares here!

Nurse: Good evening. I am Staff Nurse Kavita. I can see that you are upset. Please sit down and tell me what happened.

Relative: The doctor said the dressing should be changed daily. It is already 6 p.m., and it is still not done. The bandage is wet.

Nurse: I understand your concern. A wet dressing must be changed, and I am sorry for the delay. There were two emergency admissions this afternoon, but that should not have affected your father's care.

Relative: Yes, but he is in pain also.

Nurse: Thank you for telling me. I will check his pain right now and give the medicine prescribed by the doctor. I will change his dressing myself within the next 15 minutes.

Relative: Okay. Please make sure it does not happen again.

Nurse: Certainly. I will also inform the sister in charge so that his dressing is done every morning on time. Is there anything else you would like to tell me?

Relative: No, that's all. Thank you, Sister.

Nurse: You're welcome, Mr. Patil. Thank you for being patient. Please let me know if you have any other concerns.

Steps of handling a complaint shown in the conversation

  1. Listen calmly without interrupting or arguing
  2. Acknowledge feelings and show empathy – "I can see that you are upset"
  3. Apologise sincerely – without blaming others
  4. Get the facts
  5. Take prompt action and state a clear time
  6. Inform the person in charge and prevent recurrence
  7. Thank the person and close politely
  8. Document the complaint and the action taken

Useful phrases

  • "I understand how you feel." "I'm sorry for the inconvenience." "Let me find out what happened." "I will take care of it immediately." "Thank you for bringing this to my notice."

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain how to plan and deliver an effective presentation.
answer_html:
Introduction A presentation is a formal talk given to an audience to inform, teach or persuade, usually with the help of visual aids. Nursing students give presentations in seminars, case presentations, health education sessions, conferences and staff meetings. A good presentation needs careful planning, preparation, practice and delivery.

A. Planning (before the presentation)

1. Know your purpose

  • Decide the aim – to inform (a seminar on diabetes), to teach (a demonstration on hand washing), or to persuade (a talk to encourage blood donation)
  • Write 2–3 clear objectives

2. Know your audience

  • Their number, age, education, language and interest – a health talk to mothers in a village differs from a seminar for classmates

3. Know the time and place

  • The time allotted, the size of the room, seating, availability of a projector, microphone and power supply

4. Collect the content

  • From textbooks, journals, reliable websites and experts; note references
  • Select main points (usually not more than 3–5); use examples, case stories and statistics

B. Organising the presentation

1. Introduction (about 10–15% of time)

  • Greet the audience and introduce yourself
  • Attract attention – a question, a short story, a striking fact ("Every day, many people in India die in road accidents")
  • State the topic, objectives and plan of the talk

2. Body (about 70–80% of time)

  • Present main points in a logical order – simple to complex, problem to solution, or in time order
  • Support each point with examples, pictures, data and demonstrations
  • Use linkers to move smoothly – "Now let us look at…", "Next…", "Another important point is…"

3. Conclusion (about 10% of time)

  • Summarise the main points
  • Give a clear take-home message or call to action
  • Thank the audience and invite questions

C. Preparing visual aids

  • Slides (PowerPoint) – not more than 6 lines per slide and about 6 words per line; large font (at least 24 points); contrasting colours; pictures and diagrams rather than long paragraphs
  • Charts, flip charts, models, posters, real objects, videos
  • Visual aids should support, not replace, the speaker
  • Check that equipment works; keep a backup (pen drive, printed handouts)

D. Rehearsal

  • Practise aloud several times; time yourself
  • Practise in front of friends or a mirror; record yourself
  • Prepare cue cards with key words – do not read from a full script

E. Delivery

1. Voice

  • Speak clearly, loudly enough and at a moderate speed; use pauses for emphasis
  • Vary pitch and intonation; avoid a monotonous voice and fillers such as "umm", "actually", "basically"

2. Body language

  • Stand straight, relaxed and confident; avoid leaning or swaying
  • Maintain eye contact with all parts of the audience
  • Use natural gestures; smile; do not turn your back to the audience while reading slides

3. Language

  • Simple, correct English; explain technical terms; use the audience's language for community talks

4. Interaction

  • Ask questions, involve the audience, use demonstrations and return demonstrations

5. Managing nervousness

  • Prepare well, breathe slowly, start with a smile, focus on the message, not on yourself

F. Handling questions

  • Listen fully to the question; repeat it for the audience
  • Answer briefly and honestly; if you do not know, say "That's a good question; I will find out and tell you"
  • Stay polite even with difficult questions

G. After the presentation

  • Ask for feedback; evaluate what went well and what to improve

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Reading word for word from slides or notes
  • Crowded slides with long paragraphs and small fonts
  • Speaking too fast, too softly or in a monotonous voice
  • Turning one's back to the audience; no eye contact
  • Exceeding the time limit; skipping the conclusion
  • Using unexplained abbreviations and jargon
  • Arguing with questioners

Qualities of a good presentation

  • Clear purpose, well organised, audience-centred, within time, supported by good visuals, delivered confidently and interactively

Conclusion An effective presentation is planned around its purpose and audience, organised into an introduction, body and conclusion, supported by simple visual aids, rehearsed well, and delivered with a clear voice, confident body language and good interaction, followed by courteous handling of questions.

subject: Communicative English
question: Give phrases for agreeing and disagreeing politely.
answer_html:
Agreeing

  • "I agree with you."
  • "That's right." / "Exactly."
  • "I think so too."
  • "You have a point there."
  • "I couldn't agree more."

Partly agreeing

  • "I agree up to a point, but…"
  • "That may be true; however…"

Disagreeing politely

  • "I'm afraid I don't agree."
  • "I see your point, but…"
  • "I'm not sure about that."
  • "With respect, I think…"
  • "I see it a little differently."

Tips

  • Avoid rude expressions such as "You are wrong"
  • Give reasons for your view
  • Keep a calm, polite tone and listen to the other person

subject: Communicative English
question: Give phrases for asking and giving directions.
answer_html:
Asking for directions

  • "Excuse me, could you tell me the way to the X-ray department?"
  • "Where is the blood bank, please?"

Giving directions

  • "Go straight down this corridor."
  • "Take the lift to the second floor."
  • "Turn left at the reception."
  • "It is next to the pharmacy." / "It is opposite the canteen."
  • "It is the third door on your right."
  • "Go past the waiting hall."
  • "Follow the signboards for Radiology."

Tips

  • Use landmarks; speak slowly and clearly
  • Point in the right direction
  • Offer to accompany elderly or confused visitors

subject: Communicative English
question: Give phrases for greetings and introductions.
answer_html:
Greetings

  • Formal: "Good morning / Good afternoon / Good evening." "How do you do?"
  • Informal: "Hello!" "Hi!" "How are you?" – Reply: "I'm fine, thank you. And you?"

Introducing oneself

  • "Good morning, I am Priya, your nurse for today."
  • "May I introduce myself? I am a first-year B.Sc Nursing student."

Introducing others

  • "Sir, this is Dr Patil, the resident doctor."
  • "I would like you to meet my colleague, Sister Anita."
  • Reply: "Pleased to meet you." / "Nice to meet you."

Leave-taking

  • "Goodbye." "See you tomorrow." "Take care." "Have a nice day."

Note: "Good night" is used only when leaving at night or going to bed – it is not a greeting.

subject: Communicative English
question: Write a conversation in which a nurse gives discharge instructions to a patient.
answer_html:
Situation: Mr Ramesh, aged 45, is going home after an appendix operation. His wife is with him.

Nurse: Good morning, Mr Ramesh. I am happy to tell you that the doctor has discharged you today. May I explain how you should take care at home? Patient: Good morning, Sister. Yes, please. Nurse: First, your medicines. This is an antibiotic – take one tablet twice a day after meals for five days. This painkiller is to be taken only if you have pain, not more than three times a day. Wife: Should he complete all the antibiotic tablets even if he feels better? Nurse: Yes, please complete the full course. Stopping early can bring the infection back. Patient: What about the wound? Nurse: Keep the dressing clean and dry. Do not wet it while bathing for the next few days. The stitches will be removed when you come for your check-up next Monday. Patient: What should I eat? Nurse: Start with light, home-cooked food such as dal, rice, khichdi and fruits. Drink plenty of water. Avoid oily and spicy food for a week. Patient: When can I go back to work? Nurse: You may walk around the house from today, but avoid lifting heavy weights for about four to six weeks. The doctor will tell you when you can return to work. Wife: When should we come back to the hospital before the check-up? Nurse: Come immediately if he has fever, increasing pain, redness or pus from the wound, vomiting or constipation for more than two days. Patient: Thank you, Sister. You have explained everything clearly. Nurse: You are welcome. Here is your discharge summary and the instruction sheet in Marathi. Take care, and get well soon.

Points shown in the conversation

  • Polite greeting and taking permission
  • Clear, simple instructions in a logical order – medicines, wound care, diet, activity, warning signs, follow-up
  • Encouraging questions and answering them patiently
  • Giving written instructions in the patient's language
  • Polite closing

subject: Communicative English
question: Write a conversation between two student nurses expressing their opinions on the use of mobile phones in the clinical area.
answer_html:
Situation: Two first-year students, Neha and Rohan, discuss whether students should use mobile phones during clinical posting.

Neha: Rohan, what do you think about using mobile phones in the ward? Rohan: In my opinion, phones are very useful. We can quickly check drug information and normal values. Neha: I see your point, but I feel phones distract us from patients. Yesterday I saw a student busy on her phone while a patient was calling for help. Rohan: That's true. Using social media during duty is certainly wrong. Neha: Exactly. Also, phones can carry germs from one place to another. We touch them all the time and then touch patients. Rohan: I hadn't thought of that. But what about emergencies? Our families may need to contact us. Neha: I agree up to a point. They can call the ward phone or we can check our phones during the break. Rohan: That sounds reasonable. And taking photos of patients must never be allowed. Neha: Absolutely. That would break patient confidentiality. Rohan: So we both agree that phones should be used only for work-related purposes, in silent mode, and never for photos or social media. Neha: Yes, I couldn't agree more. Let us suggest these rules to our class coordinator. Rohan: Good idea. Let's meet her after the class.

Phrases used

  • Giving opinions: "In my opinion…", "I feel…", "What do you think about…?"
  • Agreeing: "That's true", "Exactly", "Absolutely", "I couldn't agree more"
  • Disagreeing politely: "I see your point, but…", "I agree up to a point"
  • Suggesting: "Let us…", "Good idea"

Features of a good discussion

  • Each speaker gives reasons and examples
  • They listen to each other and remain polite
  • They reach a sensible conclusion together

Language tips for discussions

  • Use "I" statements for opinions ("I feel…") rather than attacking others ("You never…")
  • Support views with facts or examples
  • Use softening words – "perhaps", "maybe", "I'm afraid"
  • Summarise what has been agreed at the end

subject: Communicative English
question: Write a dialogue in which a nurse explains a procedure to a patient and obtains his cooperation.
answer_html:
Situation: The nurse has to collect a blood sample from Mr Suresh for a blood sugar test.

Nurse: Good morning, sir. I am Kavita, the nurse on duty. Could you please tell me your full name and date of birth? Patient: Suresh Wankhede, 14 March 1970. Nurse: Thank you. The doctor has ordered a blood test to check your sugar level. I need to take a small amount of blood from a vein in your arm. Is that all right? Patient: Will it hurt? Nurse: You will feel a small prick, like an ant bite, for a few seconds. It will be over quickly. Patient: All right. What should I do? Nurse: Please sit comfortably and stretch out your left arm. I will tie this band above your elbow. Please make a fist… Good. Now I will clean the skin. Patient: Okay. Nurse: A small prick now… You are doing very well. Please open your fist slowly. Patient: That was not as bad as I thought. Nurse: It's done. Please press this cotton firmly for two minutes and do not bend your arm. You may have your breakfast now. Patient: When will the report come? Nurse: By this evening. The doctor will explain the results to you during the round. Patient: Thank you, Sister. Nurse: You're welcome. Please call me if there is any bleeding or swelling.

Points shown

  • Introduction and correct patient identification using two identifiers
  • Explanation of purpose and what the patient will feel, in simple words
  • Consent and cooperation obtained
  • Clear, step-by-step instructions using imperative sentences ("Please make a fist")
  • Encouragement and after-care instructions
  • Polite closing

Useful phrases for explaining procedures

  • "The doctor has ordered… to check…"
  • "You may feel a little…"
  • "This will take about… minutes."
  • "Please tell me if you feel any pain."
  • "You are doing very well."
  • "Do you have any questions?"

subject: Communicative English
question: Give an oral report to the ward in-charge about an incident in which a patient fell in the bathroom.
answer_html:
Situation: A student nurse reports a patient fall to the ward sister.

Oral report

"Good afternoon, Sister. I need to report an incident.

At about 2.15 pm today, Mrs Shanta Meshram, the 68-year-old patient in bed 12, who was admitted with pneumonia, slipped and fell in the bathroom.

She had gone to the bathroom alone without calling for help. The floor was wet. I heard her call out and reached her within a minute. She was sitting on the floor and was conscious and talking.

She complained of pain in her right hip. There was a small bruise on her right elbow. There was no bleeding and no head injury, as she did not hit her head.

With the help of the ward attendant, I helped her back to bed using a wheelchair. I checked her vital signs: pulse 96 per minute, BP 130/80 mmHg and SpO₂ 95%.

I have informed Dr Kulkarni, who has come to examine her and has ordered an X-ray of the hip. I have raised the side rails, kept the call bell within her reach and asked the housekeeping staff to dry the bathroom floor.

I will write the incident report and record the details in the nurses' notes. Shall I also inform her relatives?"

Features of a good oral report

  • Begins with a greeting and a clear purpose
  • Gives who, what, when, where and how in a logical order
  • Uses the past tense for events and the present tense for the current condition
  • Facts only – no guessing or blaming
  • States action taken and what still needs to be done
  • Clear, calm and brief; asks for further instructions

Useful language for oral reports

  • "I would like to report…", "At about… o'clock…"
  • "The patient complained of…", "On examination…"
  • "I have informed…", "The doctor has ordered…"
  • "I will document…", "Shall I…?"

subject: Communicative English
question: Differentiate between skimming and scanning.
answer_html:
