Introduction Skimming and scanning are fast reading techniques used for different purposes.

Skimming Scanning
reading quickly to get the general idea (gist) reading quickly to find specific information
eyes move over headings, first and last paragraphs, topic sentences eyes search for key words, numbers, names, dates
answers "What is this text about?" answers "Where is the fact I need?"
e.g. glancing through a chapter before a lecture, reading a newspaper headline e.g. finding a drug dose in a drug book, a name in the duty roster, a phone number

Both save time; for drug orders and important instructions, careful (intensive) reading is always needed.

subject: Communicative English
question: Expand the following medical abbreviations: BP, TPR, IV, IM, NPO, BD, TDS, QID, SOS, stat, HS, PRN.
answer_html:
Answer

  1. BP – blood pressure
  2. TPR – temperature, pulse, respiration
  3. IV – intravenous (into a vein)
  4. IM – intramuscular (into a muscle)
  5. NPO – nil per os (nothing by mouth)
  6. BD / BID – twice a day
  7. TDS / TID – three times a day
  8. QID / QDS – four times a day
  9. SOS – if necessary (si opus sit)
  10. Stat – immediately (statim)
  11. HS – at bedtime (hora somni)
  12. PRN – as and when required (pro re nata)

Caution: use only approved abbreviations; when in doubt, write the full word (e.g. write "units" in full, never "U").

subject: Communicative English
question: Give the meanings of the following idioms and use them in sentences: under the weather, on the mend, burn the midnight oil, a bitter pill to swallow.
answer_html:
Answer

  1. Under the weather – slightly ill
    • "Meena is feeling under the weather, so she has taken leave today."
  2. On the mend – recovering from an illness or injury
    • "After the operation, my grandfather is on the mend."
  3. Burn the midnight oil – to study or work late into the night
    • "Before the university examinations, the students burnt the midnight oil."
  4. A bitter pill to swallow – an unpleasant fact that one has to accept
    • "Losing the final match was a bitter pill to swallow for the team."

More idioms: in the pink of health (very healthy), a clean bill of health (declared healthy), back on one's feet (recovered), break the ice (start a conversation in a new group).

subject: Communicative English
question: Spot the errors and correct the following sentences, giving the rule.
answer_html:
Introduction Spotting errors means finding the grammatical mistake in a sentence and correcting it. Below are common errors made by nursing students, with corrections and the rule behind each.

  1. ✗ "He do not come on time." ✓ "He does not come on time." Rule: a singular subject (he, she, it) takes a singular verb (does).

  2. ✗ "The patient is having fever since two days." ✓ "The patient has had fever for two days." Rule: an action continuing from the past uses the present perfect; for is used with a period of time, since with a point of time (since Monday).

  3. ✗ "One of the nurse is absent." ✓ "One of the nurses is absent." Rule: "one of" is followed by a plural noun and a singular verb.

  4. ✗ "Each of the students have a uniform." ✓ "Each of the students has a uniform." Rule: each, every, either, neither take a singular verb.

  5. ✗ "She is more taller than her sister." ✓ "She is taller than her sister." Rule: do not use a double comparative.

  6. ✗ "Let us discuss about the case." ✓ "Let us discuss the case." Rule: discuss does not take about.

  7. ✗ "He returned back from duty." ✓ "He returned from duty." Rule: avoid redundancy – return already means "come back".

  8. ✗ "I am knowing the answer." ✓ "I know the answer." Rule: stative verbs (know, believe, like, understand) are not used in the continuous form.

  9. ✗ "The doctor gave me an advice." ✓ "The doctor gave me some advice (a piece of advice)." Rule: advice, information, equipment, luggage are uncountable nouns.

  10. ✗ "The patient was died last night." ✓ "The patient died last night." Rule: die is an intransitive verb; it is not used in the passive.

  11. ✗ "Myself Priya, from second year." ✓ "I am Priya, a second-year student." Rule: myself is a reflexive pronoun, not a subject.

  12. ✗ "He is senior than me." ✓ "He is senior to me." Rule: senior, junior, superior, inferior take to, not than.

Tips for spotting errors

  • Check subject–verb agreement, tense, articles (a/an/the), prepositions, pronouns, singular/plural and redundant words

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain how to read and interpret graphs, charts and tables.
answer_html:
Introduction Nurses read many visual presentations of data – TPR charts, intake–output charts, growth charts, partographs, laboratory tables, and graphs in journals and reports. Reading them correctly helps in quick decisions; misreading them can cause errors.

A. Types of visuals

  1. Line graph – shows change over time (temperature chart, growth chart)
  2. Bar graph – compares quantities (number of patients in different wards)
  3. Pie chart – shows parts of a whole as percentages
  4. Histogram – frequency distribution (ages of patients)
  5. Table – data arranged in rows and columns (laboratory results)
  6. Flow chart – steps of a process (CPR algorithm)

B. Steps in reading a visual

  1. Read the title – what the visual is about
  2. Read the labels on the axes, the units (°C, mmHg, kg, %) and the legend (key)
  3. Check the scale – each square may stand for 0.2 °C or 10 patients
  4. Look at the overall pattern – rising, falling, steady, fluctuating
  5. Find the highest and lowest values and any sudden change
  6. Compare different bars, lines or columns
  7. Draw conclusions – what does the data show?
  8. Check the source and date of the data

C. Language for describing visuals

  • Rise: increased, rose, went up, climbed, peaked at
  • Fall: decreased, fell, dropped, declined
  • No change: remained steady, stayed constant, levelled off
  • Speed: sharply, suddenly, rapidly, gradually, slightly
  • Comparison: higher than, twice as many as, the lowest

D. Example: interpreting a patient's temperature chart (illustrative)

Day Morning Evening
Day 1 38.6 °C 39.4 °C
Day 2 38.2 °C 38.6 °C
Day 3 37.4 °C 37.6 °C
Day 4 37.0 °C 37.0 °C

Interpretation: "The chart shows the patient's temperature over four days. The temperature peaked at 39.4 °C on the evening of day 1. It was higher every evening than in the morning. From day 2 it fell gradually, reaching normal (37 °C) on day 4. The fever subsided slowly, by lysis, which suggests that the treatment is working."

Conclusion Reading visuals involves checking the title, labels, units, scale and legend, finding the pattern, highest and lowest values and changes, and stating conclusions in clear language; this skill is essential for safe nursing practice.

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain how to build medical vocabulary using prefixes, suffixes and root words.
answer_html:
Introduction Medical words look difficult, but most are built from three parts: a prefix (beginning), a root (main meaning) and a suffix (ending). Knowing common parts helps nurses understand new words while reading case sheets and textbooks.

Example: peri (around) + card (heart) + itis (inflammation) = pericarditis – inflammation around the heart.

A. Common root words

Root Meaning Example
cardi / cardio heart cardiology
gastr / gastro stomach gastritis
hepat / hepato liver hepatitis
nephr / ren kidney nephritis, renal
neur / neuro nerve neuralgia
oste / osteo bone osteoporosis
pneum / pulmon lung pneumonia, pulmonary
derm / dermat skin dermatitis
haem / hem blood haemorrhage
arthr joint arthritis
cyst bladder cystitis
hyster uterus hysterectomy
ophthalm eye ophthalmology
oto ear otitis

B. Common prefixes

Prefix Meaning Example
a- / an- without apnoea, anaemia
brady- slow bradycardia
tachy- fast tachycardia
dys- difficult, painful dyspnoea, dysuria
hyper- above, excess hypertension
hypo- below, deficient hypoglycaemia
poly- many, much polyuria
peri- around pericardium
intra- within intravenous
sub- under subcutaneous
pre- / post- before / after pre-operative, post-natal
hemi- half hemiplegia

C. Common suffixes

Suffix Meaning Example
-itis inflammation appendicitis
-ectomy surgical removal appendicectomy
-otomy cutting into tracheotomy
-ostomy making an opening colostomy
-algia pain neuralgia
-aemia condition of blood anaemia, septicaemia
-uria condition of urine haematuria
-scopy looking inside endoscopy
-megaly enlargement hepatomegaly
-penia deficiency thrombocytopenia
-plasty surgical repair rhinoplasty
-logy study of pathology

Tips for building vocabulary

  • Keep a vocabulary notebook; learn 5 new words daily
  • Break unfamiliar words into parts
  • Use a medical dictionary; read aloud for correct pronunciation
  • Use new words in sentences and case presentations

Conclusion Learning common roots, prefixes and suffixes helps nurses decode and remember medical terms, making reading faster and more accurate.

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain the types of reading and the strategies for effective reading.
answer_html:
Introduction Reading is the process of looking at written symbols and understanding their meaning. It is a receptive skill. For a nurse, reading is needed every day – case sheets, drug labels, charts, notices, textbooks, journals and research articles. Good readers adjust their speed and method to their purpose.

A. Types of reading

1. Skimming

  • Quick reading to get the main idea – headings, introduction, first sentences of paragraphs, conclusion
  • Use: previewing a chapter, deciding whether an article is useful

2. Scanning

  • Quick searching for specific information – a name, number, date or key word
  • Use: finding a drug dose, a patient's bed number, an exam date on a notice

3. Intensive reading

  • Slow, careful, detailed reading for full understanding and accuracy
  • Use: doctors' orders, drug labels, examination questions, legal forms, study of textbooks

4. Extensive reading

  • Reading large amounts for general understanding and pleasure – novels, magazines, newspapers
  • Improves vocabulary, fluency and general knowledge

5. Critical reading

  • Reading with questioning and evaluation – Is it true? Is the source reliable? Is there bias?
  • Use: research articles, health news, social media messages

6. Silent and loud (oral) reading

  • Silent reading is faster and better for understanding
  • Loud reading improves pronunciation and is used when reading instructions to patients

B. Strategies for effective reading

1. Set a purpose

  • Decide why you are reading – general idea, specific facts or deep understanding

2. Preview and predict

  • Look at the title, headings, pictures and summary; guess what the text will say

3. The SQ3R method (Francis P. Robinson)

  • S – Survey: skim the chapter – headings, diagrams, summary
  • Q – Question: turn headings into questions ("What are the causes of anaemia?")
  • R – Read: read actively to find answers
  • R – Recite: say or write the answers in your own words without looking
  • R – Review: revise the whole chapter after some time

4. Use context clues for new words

  • Guess the meaning from the sentence; then confirm with a dictionary

5. Identify the main idea and supporting details

  • The topic sentence (often the first sentence) gives the main idea of a paragraph

6. Make notes

  • Underline or highlight key points (only in your own books), write margin notes, prepare summaries, mind maps and flow charts

7. Visualise

  • Form mental pictures – of organs, procedures and processes

8. Monitor understanding

  • Stop and ask yourself, "Have I understood?" Re-read difficult parts

9. Improve reading speed

  • Read in phrases (chunks), not word by word
  • Avoid regression (unnecessary going back) and sub-vocalisation (saying each word in the mind)
  • Practise regularly with timed reading

10. Read critically

  • Separate facts from opinions; check the author, date and source; compare with other sources

11. Create a good reading environment

  • Good light, comfortable posture, a quiet place, short breaks every 40–50 minutes

C. Reading notes, messages, articles and news items

  • Notes and messages – read for who, what, when, where and the action required
  • News items – the headline and first paragraph give the main facts
  • Articles – identify the writer's purpose, main arguments and conclusion

D. Importance of reading for nurses

  • Safe practice (accurate reading of orders and labels), continuing education, evidence-based practice, examination success and better writing skills

Conclusion Reading may be skimming, scanning, intensive, extensive, critical, silent or loud, depending on the purpose. Strategies such as setting a purpose, previewing, SQ3R, using context clues, finding the main idea, making notes, monitoring understanding and reading critically make reading faster, deeper and more useful for nursing practice.

subject: Communicative English
question: Expand the following abbreviations: ICU, OPD, ECG, CBC, Hb, ABG, CPR, RBS, BMI, LMP, EDD, c/o.
answer_html:
Answer

  1. ICU – Intensive Care Unit
  2. OPD – Out-Patient Department
  3. ECG – Electrocardiogram
  4. CBC – Complete Blood Count
  5. Hb – Haemoglobin
  6. ABG – Arterial Blood Gas
  7. CPR – Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation
  8. RBS – Random Blood Sugar

subject: Communicative English
question: Give the meanings of the following idioms and use them in sentences: at death's door, black and blue, go under the knife, a taste of one's own medicine.
answer_html:
Answer

  1. At death's door – very seriously ill; close to dying
    • "Grandfather was at death's door with pneumonia, but he recovered after treatment."
  2. Black and blue – badly bruised
    • "After falling from the bicycle, the boy's knees were black and blue."
  3. Go under the knife – to have a surgical operation
    • "She will go under the knife for a gall bladder operation next week."
  4. A taste of one's own medicine – the same unpleasant treatment that one has given to others
    • "The bully got a taste of his own medicine when his friends ignored him."

Note: idioms are used mainly in conversation; avoid them in formal nursing documentation.

subject: Communicative English
question: Give one-word substitutes for the following.
answer_html:
Answer

  1. Inability to sleep – Insomnia
  2. A medicine that relieves pain – Analgesic
  3. A doctor who treats children – Paediatrician
  4. A disease that spreads over a whole country or the world – Pandemic
  5. A disease that occurs in many people in a community at the same time – Epidemic
  6. Loss of memory – Amnesia
  7. A substance that prevents the growth of germs on living tissue – Antiseptic
  8. The branch of medicine dealing with the elderly – Geriatrics
  9. A disease that spreads by contact – Contagious
  10. Examination of a dead body to find the cause of death – Autopsy (post-mortem)
  11. Fear of heights – Acrophobia
  12. A doctor who gives anaesthesia – Anaesthetist

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain the rules of subject–verb agreement with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction Subject–verb agreement means that the verb must agree with its subject in number and person – a singular subject takes a singular verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb. It is one of the commonest areas of error in English.

Rules with examples

  1. Singular subject – singular verb; plural subject – plural verb

    • "The nurse checks the drip." / "The nurses check the drips."

  2. Two subjects joined by "and" take a plural verb

    • "The doctor and the nurse are in the ward."
    • Exception – when both refer to one person or idea: "The ward sister and clinical instructor is on leave." (one person holds both posts)

  3. "Either…or", "neither…nor", "or" – the verb agrees with the nearer subject

    • "Neither the patient nor his relatives were present."
    • "Either the nurses or the doctor is responsible."

  4. Each, every, either, neither, everyone, somebody, nobody – take a singular verb

    • "Each patient has a call bell." "Everyone is ready for the round."

  5. Words between the subject and the verb do not change the verb

    • "The box of gloves is on the shelf."
    • "The patient, along with his parents, was waiting."

  6. Uncountable nouns take a singular verb

    • "The equipment is clean." "This information is confidential."

  7. Nouns plural in form but singular in meaning

    • "Measles is a viral disease." "The news is good."

  8. Amounts of money, time and distance treated as one unit take a singular verb

    • "Eight hours is a long shift." "Five hundred rupees is the fee."

  9. "The number of" takes a singular verb; "a number of" takes a plural verb

    • "The number of patients is increasing."
    • "A number of patients are waiting."

  10. "One of the" + plural noun takes a singular verb

    • "One of the nurses is absent today."

  11. "There is / there are" – the verb agrees with the noun that follows

    • "There are two patients in the queue." "There is a bed free."

  12. Collective nouns – usually singular when the group acts as one unit

    • "The team is efficient."

Practice (with answers)

  1. The list of patients ~~are~~ is on the table.
  2. Neither the doctor nor the nurses ~~was~~ were informed.
  3. Every student ~~have~~ has a uniform.
  4. Diabetes ~~are~~ is common in India.

Conclusion Verbs must agree with their subjects in number; special care is needed with "either/neither", indefinite pronouns, uncountable nouns, collective nouns and phrases between the subject and the verb.

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain the use of prepositions with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction A preposition is a word placed before a noun or pronoun to show its relation to another word in the sentence – in place, time, direction, manner and so on. Many errors in Indian English involve prepositions.

1. Prepositions of time

  • At – exact time: at 8 am, at night, at noon
  • On – days and dates: on Monday, on 5 June
  • In – months, years, seasons, parts of the day: in July, in 2026, in the morning
  • Since – a point of time (with perfect tenses): "He has been in the ICU since Monday."
  • For – a period of time: "He has had fever for three days."
  • By – not later than: "Send the report by 5 pm."
  • During, before, after, until

2. Prepositions of place

  • At – a point: at the nursing station, at the door
  • In – inside an enclosed space: in the ward, in the drawer
  • On – on a surface: on the bed, on the trolley
  • Under, above, below, behind, in front of, opposite
  • Beside (next to) – "Keep the stool beside the bed."; besides (in addition to) – "Besides fever, he has cough."
  • Between (two) – between the two beds; among (more than two) – among the patients

3. Prepositions of direction and movement

  • To – "Take him to the OT."
  • Into – "Wheel the patient into the room."
  • From, towards, through, across, along, out of

4. Other uses

  • By – agent or means: "The dressing was done by the nurse." "He came by ambulance."
  • With – instrument or accompaniment: "Clean the wound with saline."
  • For – purpose: "This tablet is for pain."

5. Fixed prepositions with certain words

  • suffer from (fever), allergic to (penicillin), admitted to (the ward), discharged from (hospital), complain of (pain), responsible for, depend on, aware of, interested in, good at, prefer tea to coffee, angry with a person

6. Common errors

  • "He is suffering with fever." → "He is suffering from fever."
  • "We reached to the hospital." → "We reached the hospital." (no preposition)
  • "She entered into the room." → "She entered the room."
  • "He is afraid from injections." → "He is afraid of injections."
  • "She is married with a doctor." → "She is married to a doctor."

Conclusion Prepositions show relationships of time, place, direction and means; nurses should learn the correct prepositions, especially fixed ones such as "suffer from" and "allergic to", for accurate speaking and writing.

subject: Communicative English
question: Read the following news item and answer the questions.
answer_html:
Passage

Dengue cases rise after monsoon

Health officials in the district have reported a sharp rise in dengue cases after heavy rains this month. Most cases came from areas where water had collected in coolers, old tyres and uncovered drums. Dengue is spread by the Aedes mosquito, which bites during the daytime and breeds in clean, stagnant water. Health workers have started a house-to-house survey to destroy breeding sites and spray insecticide. Doctors have advised people with high fever, severe body ache, pain behind the eyes or a skin rash to visit the nearest health centre, and to avoid painkillers other than paracetamol. People are requested to empty and dry all water containers at least once a week and to use mosquito nets and full-sleeved clothes.

Questions and answers

  1. Which mosquito spreads dengue, and when does it bite?

    • Dengue is spread by the Aedes mosquito, which bites during the daytime.

  2. Where did most cases come from?

    • From areas where water had collected in coolers, old tyres and uncovered drums.

  3. What symptoms should make a person visit the health centre?

    • High fever, severe body ache, pain behind the eyes or a skin rash.

  4. Which painkiller is advised?

    • Only paracetamol; other painkillers should be avoided.

  5. Give two measures people can take to prevent dengue.

    • Empty and dry water containers at least once a week; use mosquito nets and full-sleeved clothes.

  6. Find a word in the passage that means "not flowing".

    • Stagnant

How to answer comprehension questions

  • Read the passage twice – first for the general idea (skimming), then for details (scanning)
  • Read the questions and underline key words
  • Find the answer in the passage; write it in your own words, in complete sentences
  • For vocabulary questions, use the context to guess the meaning
  • Do not add information that is not in the passage

Vocabulary from the passage

  • Breeds – produces young ones; multiplies
  • Insecticide – a chemical that kills insects
  • Survey – a careful examination or inspection of an area or group
  • Stagnant – not flowing; still

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain how to read and interpret a laboratory report, with the example of a complete blood count.
answer_html:
Introduction Nurses read laboratory reports every day. Correct reading helps them recognise abnormal results, inform the doctor in time and plan care. Every report has the patient's details, test names, results, units and reference (normal) ranges.

A. Steps in reading a report

  1. Check patient identity – name, age, sex, hospital number, ward
  2. Note the date and time of the sample and the type of sample
  3. Read each test name, result and unit
  4. Compare each result with the reference range printed beside it (ranges vary slightly between laboratories)
  5. Look for flags – H (high), L (low) or a star – and critical values
  6. Compare with earlier reports to see the trend
  7. Report abnormal and critical values to the doctor at once and document the communication

B. Example – complete blood count (CBC) of a 32-year-old woman

Test Result Reference range Flag
Haemoglobin 8.6 g/dl 12–15 g/dl L
Total WBC count 13,500 /µl 4,000–11,000 /µl H
Neutrophils 82% 40–80% H
Lymphocytes 14% 20–40% L
Platelet count 2.1 lakh /µl 1.5–4.0 lakh /µl normal
MCV 70 fl 83–101 fl L

C. Interpretation in simple words

  • Low haemoglobin with low MCV – the red cells are small; this suggests anaemia, probably due to iron deficiency
  • High WBC count with high neutrophils – suggests a bacterial infection
  • Platelets normal – no bleeding risk from platelets

D. Nursing actions

  • Inform the doctor about the low haemoglobin and raised WBC count
  • Observe for signs of anaemia (pallor, breathlessness, tiredness) and infection (fever, wound or urinary symptoms)
  • Give iron-rich diet advice and prescribed treatment; repeat tests as ordered
  • Document the findings and the time the doctor was informed

E. Language points

  • Learn the units (g/dl, /µl, %, fl) and common abbreviations (Hb, WBC, MCV)
  • Use words such as "within normal limits", "raised", "low", "markedly elevated" when reporting

Conclusion Reading a report involves checking identity, test, result, unit and reference range, noticing flags and trends, and reporting abnormal values promptly; the CBC example shows how numbers are turned into meaningful nursing information.

subject: Communicative English
question: What is an anecdotal record? Mention its characteristics.
answer_html:
Definition An anecdotal record is a brief, factual, written description of a specific incident or behaviour of a person (a student or a patient), recorded by an observer soon after it happens.

Characteristics

  1. Describes one specific incident
  2. Objective – states what was seen and heard, not opinions
  3. Written soon after the event
  4. Includes date, time, place and the persons involved
  5. Brief and clear
  6. The observer's interpretation or comment is written separately from the description
  7. Collected over a period, it shows a pattern of behaviour

Use: evaluation of students' clinical behaviour and attitudes; observing patients' behaviour.

subject: Communicative English
question: What is an abstract? Mention its parts.
answer_html:
Definition An abstract is a brief summary of a research paper, thesis or article, usually 150–300 words, which tells the reader what was studied, how, what was found and what it means.

Parts of an abstract

  1. Background / introduction – why the study was done
  2. Objectives – what the study aimed to find
  3. Methods – design, sample, setting, tools
  4. Results – main findings with key figures
  5. Conclusion – meaning and implications
  6. Keywords – 3–6 words for indexing

Features: written in the past tense, clear, concise, without references or abbreviations that are not explained.

subject: Communicative English
question: Mention the parts of a formal letter.
answer_html:
Introduction A formal letter is written for official purposes – applications, requests, complaints.

Parts of a formal letter

  1. Sender's address
  2. Date
  3. Receiver's designation and address ("To, The Principal, …")
  4. Subject – one line stating the purpose
  5. Salutation – "Respected Sir/Madam" or "Dear Sir/Madam"
  6. Body – introduction, main matter and conclusion (usually three short paragraphs)
  7. Complimentary close – "Yours faithfully" or "Yours sincerely"
  8. Signature and name, with class or designation
  9. Enclosures (if any) – e.g. "Encl: Medical certificate"

subject: Communicative English
question: What is a reflective diary (journal)? Mention its uses.
answer_html:
Definition A reflective diary (journal) is a personal written record of one's daily experiences, thoughts, feelings and learning, written regularly. Nursing students write clinical reflective journals about their ward experiences.

Format (a simple model): what happened → what I felt → what went well and what did not → what I learnt → what I will do next time.

Uses

  1. Develops self-awareness and reflective thinking
  2. Helps learning from experience – linking theory with practice
  3. Improves writing skills and expression
  4. Helps manage stress by expressing feelings
  5. Records progress in clinical skills
  6. Helps teachers understand and guide students

question: Write a report on a health education programme on anaemia conducted by your college in a nearby village.
answer_html:
Format: a short event report – title, introduction, details, outcome, conclusion, name and date.

Report on a Health Education Programme on Anaemia at Village Mohgaon

Reported by: Rohan Meshram, Second Year B.Sc. Nursing, XYZ College of Nursing

Introduction The Department of Community Health Nursing of XYZ College of Nursing organised a health education programme on "Prevention of Anaemia in Women and Adolescent Girls" at the Gram Panchayat hall of Village Mohgaon on 8 November 2026, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. The programme was conducted in collaboration with the Primary Health Centre and the village anganwadi worker.

Participants About 85 women and adolescent girls attended. The sarpanch, the medical officer of the PHC, two faculty members and 30 nursing students were present.

Programme details The programme began with a welcome speech by the class representative. The medical officer explained the causes and effects of anaemia. Nursing students presented a role play showing a tired, pale girl who improves after eating iron-rich food and taking iron tablets. A health talk with flip charts explained iron-rich local foods such as green leafy vegetables, jaggery, groundnuts and sprouted pulses, the importance of vitamin C, deworming and avoiding tea with meals. Haemoglobin was checked for 60 participants with a digital haemoglobinometer, and those with low levels were referred to the PHC. Iron and folic acid tablets were distributed by the ASHA worker as per the national programme.

Outcome Participants asked many questions and took part actively in a quiz at the end. Pamphlets in Marathi were distributed.

Conclusion The programme was successful in creating awareness about anaemia. The students suggested follow-up visits after three months. The programme ended with a vote of thanks by a student.

Date: 9 November 2026 Signature: (Rohan Meshram)

Features of a good report: a clear title, the 5 Ws and H (what, when, where, who, why, how), past tense, objective and factual language, logical order, brief, signed and dated.

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain the methods of note taking.
answer_html:
Introduction Note taking is writing down the main points while listening to a lecture or presentation; note making is writing the main points while reading a book or article. Good notes help in understanding, remembering and revising for examinations.

Methods of note taking

1. Cornell method (developed at Cornell University)

  • Divide the page into three parts:
    • Note-taking column (right, large) – notes during the lecture
    • Cue column (left, narrow) – key words and questions added after the lecture
    • Summary area (bottom) – a short summary of the page
  • Merit: excellent for revision – cover the notes and answer the cues

2. Outline method

  • Main headings, sub-headings and points arranged with numbers and indentation:
      1. Anaemia
    • a. Definition
    • b. Types – (i) iron deficiency, (ii) megaloblastic
  • Merit: shows the relationship between ideas clearly

3. Mapping (mind map) method

  • The main topic is written in the centre; branches show sub-topics and details; colours and pictures may be used
  • Merit: visual; good for creative thinkers and quick revision

4. Charting (table) method

  • Information is arranged in columns – e.g. drug name, action, dose, side effects, nursing care
  • Merit: useful for comparing facts

5. Sentence method

  • Each new fact is written as a separate numbered sentence
  • Merit: simple; useful when the lecture is fast; limitation: does not show relationships

6. Flow-chart method

  • Steps of processes shown with boxes and arrows (e.g. blood clotting, nursing process)

Tips for good notes

  • Write key words and phrases, not full sentences
  • Use abbreviations and symbols: ↑ increase, ↓ decrease, → leads to, ∴ therefore, ∵ because, w/ with, w/o without, e.g. for example
  • Leave space to add points later
  • Date and title each page
  • Review and complete notes the same day

Conclusion Cornell, outline, mapping, charting, sentence and flow-chart methods help students record lectures efficiently; regular review turns good notes into lasting learning.

subject: Communicative English
question: Write the history of a patient admitted with fever.
answer_html:
Introduction A patient history is a systematic written record of the patient's personal details, complaints and past and present health, collected by interview. It must be accurate, complete, clear and in the correct order.

Patient History (sample)

1. Identification data

  • Name: Mrs. Lata Bhoyar | Age: 34 years | Sex: Female
  • IP No.: 2456 | Ward: Female Medical Ward, Bed 12
  • Address: Village Khapa, Tal. Saoner, Dist. Nagpur
  • Religion: Hindu | Education: 10th standard | Occupation: Housewife
  • Marital status: Married | Date of admission: 10 November 2026
  • Diagnosis: Fever under evaluation (?malaria)

2. Chief complaints (with duration)

  • Fever with chills – 4 days
  • Headache and body ache – 3 days
  • Vomiting – 2 days

3. History of present illness

  • The patient was apparently well 4 days ago, when she developed fever with chills and rigors, mainly in the evening, followed by sweating. The fever came every alternate day. She took paracetamol from a local medical shop with temporary relief. For the last 2 days she has had vomiting (3–4 times a day) and is unable to eat. There is no cough, burning micturition or loose motions.

4. Past medical and surgical history

  • No history of diabetes, hypertension, tuberculosis or asthma
  • No previous hospital admission or surgery

5. Drug and allergy history

  • Paracetamol tablets for 4 days; no known drug allergy

6. Family history

  • Husband, 38 years, farmer, healthy; two children, healthy
  • Her neighbour was treated for malaria last month

7. Personal history

  • Diet: mixed; appetite reduced
  • Sleep: disturbed due to fever
  • Bowel: regular; Bladder: normal
  • Habits: no tobacco or alcohol

8. Menstrual and obstetric history

  • Menstrual cycle regular, 28–30 days; last menstrual period 25 October 2026
  • Obstetric score: G2 P2 L2; both normal deliveries

9. Socio-economic history

  • Joint family; monthly family income from farming; lives in a kutcha house near a pond; does not use a mosquito net

Points to remember

  • Write in the past tense, in the third person
  • Record complaints in chronological order with duration
  • Use the patient's own words for symptoms where useful
  • Be objective; write legibly; sign with date

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain summarising and the steps of writing a summary.
answer_html:
Introduction Summarising is writing the main ideas of a passage in a short form, in one's own words. A précis is a formal summary, usually about one-third of the original length, with a title. Nurses summarise when they write discharge summaries, case summaries, handover notes and abstracts.

Qualities of a good summary

  1. Brief – much shorter than the original
  2. Complete – includes all the main ideas
  3. Clear and coherent – ideas flow logically
  4. Objective – no personal opinions or new information
  5. In one's own words – not copied

Steps in writing a summary

  1. Read the passage carefully two or three times to understand it fully
  2. Find the central idea – what is the passage mainly about?
  3. Underline or list the key points
  4. Leave out examples, illustrations, repetitions, quotations, figures of speech and minor details
  5. Write a rough draft in your own words, joining the points with linkers
  6. Use reported speech and the third person; keep the same tense as the original
  7. Check the length – about one-third of the original for a précis
  8. Compare with the original to make sure no main point is missed and nothing is added
  9. Give a suitable title (for a précis)
  10. Write the final copy neatly

Example

  • Original (about 60 words): "Hand washing is the simplest and most effective way to prevent the spread of infection in hospitals. Germs on the hands of health workers can pass from one patient to another. If every nurse and doctor washed hands before and after touching each patient, many hospital infections could be prevented, saving lives and money."
  • Summary (about 20 words): "Hand washing by health workers before and after patient contact is the simplest, most effective way to prevent hospital infections."

Conclusion A summary presents the main ideas of a passage briefly, clearly and objectively in one's own words; careful reading, selecting key points, omitting details and checking against the original are the steps to a good summary.

subject: Communicative English
question: Define a report. Explain the types, structure and qualities of a good report, with an example.
answer_html:
(a) Definition

  • A report is a systematic, organised and factual account of an event, activity, investigation or situation, prepared for a specific purpose and reader
  • It usually ends with conclusions and sometimes recommendations
  • In nursing, reports include ward reports, incident reports, shift reports, transfer reports, reports of health camps, inspection reports and research reports

(b) Types of reports

1. According to presentation

  • Oral report – given in speech (change-of-shift handover, telephone report to the doctor)
  • Written report – documented (incident report, annual report)

2. According to formality

  • Formal report – follows a fixed format; for official use (investigation report)
  • Informal report – a short memo or letter report

3. According to frequency

  • Routine (periodic) reports – at regular intervals: daily ward report, monthly statistics, annual report
  • Special reports – for a particular event: incident report, report of a fire drill, report of a health camp

4. According to purpose

  • Informational report – presents facts only (number of admissions)
  • Analytical (investigative) report – analyses facts and gives conclusions and recommendations (report on causes of patient falls)

5. According to length

  • Short reports (1–2 pages) and long reports (research reports, project reports)

(c) Structure (format) of a report

For a long, formal report

  1. Title page – title, prepared for, prepared by, date
  2. Contents (for long reports)
  3. Executive summary / abstract – a brief summary of the whole report
  4. Introduction – background, purpose and scope
  5. Method – how information was collected (observation, interviews, records)
  6. Findings (body) – facts presented in a logical order with headings, tables and figures
  7. Conclusions – what the findings mean
  8. Recommendations – suggested actions
  9. References and appendices
  10. Signature, name, designation and date

For a short event report

  • Heading → introduction (what, when, where, who organised, why) → details of activities in order → outcome → conclusion / recommendations → name, signature and date

(d) Qualities of a good report

  1. Accuracy – correct facts, figures, names and times
  2. Objectivity – facts, not personal feelings or blame
  3. Clarity – simple, clear language; technical terms explained
  4. Brevity – no unnecessary details
  5. Completeness – answers what, when, where, who, why and how
  6. Logical order – headings, numbered points
  7. Timeliness – written promptly while facts are fresh
  8. Proper format – as required by the organisation
  9. Correct grammar and spelling; usually past tense and often the passive voice ("A fire drill was conducted")
  10. Signed and dated by the writer

(e) Example: a short special report

Report on the Fire Safety Drill held in the Surgical Ward

To: The Nursing Superintendent From: Sister In-charge, Surgical Ward Date: 5 November 2026

Introduction: A fire safety drill was conducted in the Surgical Ward on 4 November 2026 from 3 p.m. to 3.45 p.m. by the hospital fire safety officer, to train the staff in the response to a fire.

Details: Twelve staff nurses, eight nursing students and four ward attendants took part. The fire officer explained the RACE (Rescue, Alarm, Contain, Extinguish or Evacuate) and PASS (Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep) methods. A mock fire was announced near the store room. The alarm was raised within one minute, the oxygen supply valve to the area was shown to the staff, and patients were evacuated to the next ward in about ten minutes. Each participant practised using a fire extinguisher.

Findings: Most staff responded correctly. However, the fire exit door near the store room was partly blocked by empty cartons, and two new staff members did not know the location of the fire extinguisher.

Recommendations: (1) The fire exit must be kept clear at all times. (2) All new staff should be oriented to fire safety on joining. (3) Drills should be held every six months.

(Signature) Sister In-charge, Surgical Ward

Conclusion A report is a factual, organised account written for a specific purpose. Reports may be oral or written, formal or informal, routine or special, informational or analytical. A good report follows a clear structure – introduction, findings, conclusions and recommendations – and is accurate, objective, clear, brief, complete, timely, signed and dated.

subject: Communicative English
question: What is a memo? Mention its format.
answer_html:
Definition A memo (memorandum) is a short, formal written message used for communication within an organisation – to inform, instruct, request or remind.

Format

  1. Name of the organisation
  2. Heading – MEMORANDUM
  3. To: (receiver's name and designation)
  4. From: (sender's name and designation)
  5. Date
  6. Subject: (brief and clear)
  7. Body – purpose, details, action required and deadline, in short paragraphs
  8. Initials or signature of the sender
  9. Copy to (cc), if needed

Note: a memo usually has no salutation ("Dear Sir") and no complimentary close.

Example: a memo from the Nursing Superintendent to all ward in-charges about a hand hygiene audit.

subject: Communicative English
question: What is a curriculum vitae (CV)? Mention its components.
answer_html:
Definition A curriculum vitae (CV) is a written summary of a person's education, qualifications, experience, skills and achievements, sent with a job application. A resume is a shorter version (one or two pages) suited to a particular job.

Components

  1. Personal details – name, address, phone number, e-mail
  2. Career objective – one or two lines
  3. Educational qualifications – latest first, with institution, year and marks or grade
  4. Professional registration – State Nursing Council registration number
  5. Work experience, including internship
  6. Clinical skills and certificates (e.g. Basic Life Support)
  7. Achievements, co-curricular activities and languages known
  8. References (two persons)
  9. Declaration, place, date and signature

  • Internship: Six months in medical, surgical, paediatric and ICU wards
  • Skills: vital signs monitoring, IV cannulation, medication administration, BLS
  • Languages: English, Marathi, Hindi
  • References: Principal and Clinical Instructor, XYZ College of Nursing
  • Declaration: I declare that the above information is true. Place, date, signature

Points to remember

  • Use the formal letter format – sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation, body, complimentary close, signature
  • Keep it brief, polite and specific; mention qualifications relevant to the post
  • Check spelling and grammar carefully

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Writing to "Dear Friend" or using informal language
  • Forgetting the date, subject line or signature
  • Copying a long, general letter that does not mention the post
  • Spelling errors in names and addresses
  • Not listing the enclosures

subject: Communicative English
question: Write an anecdotal record on the behaviour of a student nurse observed in the clinical area.
answer_html:
What to include in an anecdotal record

  • Name of the person observed, date, time and place
  • Objective description of the incident – exactly what happened, without opinion
  • Interpretation (comment) written separately
  • Recommendation, if any
  • Name and signature of the observer

Sample anecdotal record

Item Details
Name of student Pooja M. (First Year B.Sc Nursing)
Area Female Medical Ward
Date and time 18 November 2026, 10.30 am
Observer Clinical Instructor

Incident (description) While giving a bed bath to a 70-year-old patient with paralysis, Pooja noticed that the patient was shivering. She immediately closed the window, covered the patient with a blanket and continued the bath one part at a time, keeping the rest of the body covered. She explained each step to the patient in Marathi and checked the skin over the hips and heels. She found a reddened area over the sacrum and reported it to the staff nurse, who started two-hourly turning. Pooja recorded the finding in the nurses' notes.

Interpretation (comment) The student showed sensitivity to the patient's comfort and privacy, good observation skills, effective communication and prompt reporting.

Recommendation She may be appreciated in the group and encouraged to share her experience in the clinical conference.

Signature of observer: ______

Points to remember

  • Record soon after the incident
  • Write facts first, opinion separately
  • Record both positive and negative behaviour; one incident per record
  • Keep records confidential

Objective and subjective statements

  • Objective (correct): "She covered the patient with a blanket and explained each step in Marathi."
  • Subjective (avoid in the description): "She is a very kind and wonderful student."
  • Opinions belong only in the interpretation section

Uses of anecdotal records

  • Give a true picture of a student's behaviour over time
  • Help in guidance, feedback and fair evaluation
  • Identify students who need extra support

subject: Communicative English
question: Write a reflective diary entry on your first day of clinical posting.
answer_html:
Structure of reflection (Gibbs' reflective cycle)

  1. Description – what happened?
  2. Feelings – what was I thinking and feeling?
  3. Evaluation – what was good and bad about the experience?
  4. Analysis – what sense can I make of it?
  5. Conclusion – what else could I have done?
  6. Action plan – what will I do next time?

Sample diary entry

Date: 4 November 2026 Place: Male Surgical Ward

Description: Today was my first day of clinical posting. After the morning report, our clinical instructor showed us the ward. I was asked to check the temperature, pulse and respiration of four patients and to help the staff nurse with a dressing.

Feelings: I was excited but nervous. My hands shook when I first touched a patient, and I was afraid of making a mistake. When an elderly patient smiled and said "Thank you, beti", I felt happy and confident.

Evaluation: I measured the vital signs correctly and recorded them neatly. However, I took too long counting the pulse and forgot to explain the procedure to one patient before starting.

Analysis: I was nervous because the setting was new. I realised that explaining a procedure reduces the patient's anxiety and also makes me calmer.

Conclusion: I should have introduced myself and explained the procedure to every patient.

Action plan: I will practise counting the pulse in the skill lab, revise the steps of dressing, and always greet and explain before any procedure.

Uses of a reflective diary

  • Improves self-awareness and learning from experience
  • Develops critical thinking and writing skills
  • Helps teachers understand students' needs

Tips for writing reflections

  • Write soon after the experience, while the details are fresh
  • Be honest about mistakes and feelings – reflection is for learning, not for blame
  • Focus on what you learned and what you will do differently
  • Protect patient confidentiality – do not write patients' names
  • Use the first person ("I felt…", "I learned…") and the past tense for events

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain the structure (format) of a scientific paper and the steps in writing it. (2 + 5 + 3)
answer_html:
(a) Introduction (2 marks)

  • A scientific (research) paper is a written report of an original study, published in a journal or presented at a conference
  • It shares new knowledge with other professionals and supports evidence-based practice
  • Nurses write papers on research projects, case studies and quality improvement work for journals such as The Nursing Journal of India
  • Most papers follow the IMRAD format – Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion

(b) Structure of a scientific paper (5 marks)

1. Title

  • Short, specific and informative; includes the main variables and population
  • Example: "Effect of structured teaching on knowledge of hand hygiene among first-year nursing students"

2. Authors and affiliations

  • Names, designations, institutions and the corresponding author's contact

3. Abstract

  • A summary of about 150–300 words, often under headings – background, objectives, methods, results, conclusion
  • Followed by 3–6 keywords

4. Introduction

  • Background of the problem, what is already known, the gap in knowledge, the need for the study and the objectives or hypotheses

5. Methods (materials and methods)

  • Research design, setting, sample and sampling technique, tools, data collection procedure, ethical approval and informed consent, and methods of data analysis

6. Results

  • Findings presented in logical order with tables and figures; facts only, without interpretation

7. Discussion

  • Interpretation of findings, comparison with other studies, strengths and limitations, and implications for nursing practice, education, administration and research

8. Conclusion and recommendations

9. Acknowledgements, funding and conflict of interest

10. References

  • In a standard style – Vancouver (numbered) or APA (author–date)

(c) Steps in writing a paper (3 marks)

  1. Choose the target journal and read its "instructions to authors"
  2. Prepare tables and figures first and make an outline
  3. Write the methods and results first, then the discussion and introduction, and finally the abstract and title
  4. Cite sources correctly; avoid plagiarism – paraphrase in your own words and acknowledge others' work
  5. Language:
    • past tense for methods and results ("Data were collected…")
    • present tense for accepted facts ("Hand hygiene reduces infection")
    • short, clear sentences; define abbreviations at first use
  6. Revise several times; ask a teacher or colleague to review
  7. Obtain all authors' approval; submit with a covering letter; respond politely to reviewers' comments

Qualities of a good scientific paper

  • Original, accurate and honest
  • Clear, concise and logically organised
  • Ethical – confidentiality of participants maintained
  • Properly referenced

(d) Sample structured abstract

  • Background: Hand hygiene is the most effective measure to prevent health care-associated infections, yet compliance among students is often poor.
  • Objective: To assess the effect of structured teaching on the knowledge of hand hygiene among first-year nursing students.
  • Methods: A one-group pre-test post-test design was used with 60 students selected by convenience sampling. Knowledge was measured with a structured questionnaire before and seven days after teaching.
  • Results: The mean knowledge score rose from 11.2 to 17.8 (out of 20); the difference was statistically significant.
  • Conclusion: Structured teaching improved knowledge of hand hygiene.
  • Keywords: hand hygiene, structured teaching, nursing students

Ethics in publication

  • Plagiarism – copying others' words or ideas without acknowledgement
  • Fabrication (inventing data) and falsification (changing data)
  • Duplicate publication – publishing the same study twice
  • Authorship – only those who contributed substantially should be authors

Common reasons papers are rejected

  • Unclear objectives or weak methods
  • Conclusions not supported by the results
  • Poor language, missing references, not following the journal's format

Conclusion A scientific paper follows the IMRAD structure – title, abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusion and references – and is written step by step, with accurate data, clear language and honest acknowledgement of sources.

subject: Communicative English
question: Define critical thinking. Mention two strategies each for critical listening and critical reading.
answer_html:
Definition Critical thinking is the careful, logical and open-minded analysis and evaluation of information, ideas and arguments in order to form a sound judgement or decision.

Strategies for critical listening

  1. Separate facts from opinions – "Is the speaker giving evidence or only a view?"
  2. Question the message – ask for reasons, sources and examples; notice exaggeration and emotional appeals

Strategies for critical reading

  1. Check the source – author, date, publisher, evidence; prefer reliable sources (textbooks, journals, WHO, Ministry of Health)
  2. Look for bias and assumptions; compare with other sources before accepting a claim (for example, health messages forwarded on social media)

subject: Communicative English
question: What is an oral report? Mention its features.
answer_html:
Definition An oral report is a spoken presentation of facts about an event, situation, patient or topic, given to an individual or a group – e.g. a change-of-shift report, a case presentation or a report of a field visit.

Features

  1. Has a clear purpose and a planned order – introduction, main points, conclusion
  2. Brief and factual, with exact figures and times
  3. Delivered in a clear voice at a suitable speed
  4. Uses notes or cue cards, and visuals when needed
  5. Time-bound
  6. Allows questions and feedback
  7. Uses formal, polite language

subject: Communicative English
question: Write instructions for a patient on how to use a metered-dose inhaler.
answer_html:
Principles of writing instructions

  • A clear title; numbered steps in the correct order
  • Short sentences beginning with an action verb ("Shake", "Breathe")
  • Simple words, the patient's language, and pictures where possible
  • Warnings and important points highlighted
  • Tell the patient what to do if something goes wrong

How to Use Your Inhaler (Metered-Dose Inhaler)

Before you start

  • Check the name and expiry date of the inhaler.
  • If it is new or has not been used for a week, spray one puff into the air.

Steps

  1. Remove the cap and check that the mouthpiece is clean.
  2. Shake the inhaler well 4–5 times.
  3. Sit or stand up straight.
  4. Breathe out fully, away from the inhaler.
  5. Place the mouthpiece between your teeth and close your lips tightly around it.
  6. Start breathing in slowly and deeply through your mouth, and press the canister once at the same time.
  7. Keep breathing in slowly until your lungs are full.
  8. Remove the inhaler and hold your breath for about 10 seconds (or as long as is comfortable).
  9. Breathe out slowly.
  10. If a second puff is advised, wait 30–60 seconds and repeat steps 2–9.
  11. Replace the cap.
  12. If your inhaler contains a steroid, rinse your mouth with water and spit it out.

Important points

  • Use the inhaler exactly as advised by your doctor; do not stop it on your own.
  • If you find it hard to press and breathe in at the same time, ask the nurse about a spacer.
  • Clean the mouthpiece once a week with warm water and let it dry.
  • Seek help immediately if your breathlessness does not improve after using your reliever inhaler, or if your lips turn blue.

Conclusion Good instructions use a clear title, numbered steps starting with action verbs, simple language and highlighted warnings, so that the patient can follow them safely at home.

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain the critical thinking strategies for listening and reading.
answer_html:
Introduction Critical thinking is the careful, logical and open-minded analysis and evaluation of information to make sound judgements. Today nurses receive information from many sources – lectures, colleagues, patients, books, the internet and social media – and not all of it is correct. Critical thinking in listening and reading helps nurses accept what is reliable and reject what is not, which is the basis of evidence-based practice.

A. Critical thinking strategies for listening

  1. Identify the purpose – is the speaker informing, persuading or selling something?
  2. Find the main idea and the supporting points
  3. Separate facts from opinions – facts can be checked; opinions are beliefs
  4. Evaluate evidence – are examples, data and sources given?
  5. Notice bias, exaggeration and emotional appeals ("This medicine cures all diseases in 3 days!")
  6. Ask questions – "How do you know?", "What is the source?", "Are there other explanations?"
  7. Listen to all sides before forming a view
  8. Summarise what was said in your own words to check understanding

B. Critical thinking strategies for reading

  1. Preview – title, author, date, publisher; is the source reliable and current?
  2. Identify the author's purpose and intended readers
  3. Identify the main argument and the reasons given
  4. Check the evidence – research studies, statistics, references; are they relevant and sufficient?
  5. Distinguish fact, opinion and assumption
  6. Look for bias – commercial interest, one-sided arguments, missing information
  7. Check logic and consistency – do the conclusions follow from the evidence?
  8. Compare with other sources – textbooks, standard guidelines (WHO, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, ICMR)
  9. Consider alternative views
  10. Apply and reflect – "How does this apply to my patients?", "So what?"

C. Example

  • A message on social media says, "Drinking hot water with lemon cures dengue."
  • A critical reader asks: Who wrote it? What is the evidence? Do official guidelines say this? She finds no evidence, does not forward it, and teaches patients the correct preventive measures and warning signs.

D. Importance for nurses

  • Safe clinical decisions, evidence-based practice, protection of patients from misinformation, better examination answers and professional growth

Conclusion Critical listening and reading involve identifying the purpose and main idea, separating facts from opinions, evaluating evidence and sources, detecting bias, checking logic and comparing with reliable sources before accepting information.

subject: Communicative English
question: Explain error analysis in LSRW skills, with common errors and ways to correct them.
answer_html:
Introduction Error analysis is the systematic study of the errors made by language learners in listening, speaking, reading and writing, to find out what errors are made, why they occur and how to correct them. It treats errors as a natural part of learning and as a guide to teaching.

Error and mistake

  • An error is systematic and due to lack of knowledge of a rule (the learner repeats it and cannot correct it himself)
  • A mistake is an occasional slip due to carelessness, tiredness or haste (the learner can correct it when pointed out)

Steps of error analysis

  1. Collect samples of the learner's speech and writing
  2. Identify the errors
  3. Classify them – pronunciation, grammar, vocabulary, spelling, punctuation
  4. Explain the causes
  5. Evaluate their seriousness – does the error affect meaning or safety?
  6. Plan remedial teaching and practice

Causes of errors

  • Mother tongue influence (interference) – applying rules and sounds of Marathi, Hindi or another language to English
  • Over-generalisation – "He goed" (applying the -ed rule to an irregular verb)
  • Incomplete learning of rules
  • Word-for-word translation – "Do one thing" (common in Indian English)
  • Faulty teaching or learning materials
  • Anxiety, haste and carelessness

A. Errors in listening

  • Missing key details – numbers, units, times (fifteen and fifty; 0.5 mg and 5 mg)
  • Confusing similar-sounding words – hyper- and hypo-; ileum and ilium; look-alike, sound-alike drug names
  • Misunderstanding accents or fast speech
  • Not listening to the full message before acting

Correction: active listening, read-back of telephone orders, asking for repetition and spelling of drug names, writing down immediately, listening practice with different accents.

B. Errors in speaking

  • Pronunciation:
    • confusion of v and w ("wery" for very)
    • adding a vowel before s-clusters ("iskool" for school, "ishtation" for station)
    • z pronounced as j ("jero" for zero)
    • pronouncing silent letters – the p in pneumonia and psychology, the b in debt, the k in knee
    • wrong word stress – de-VEL-op (correct), not DE-ve-lop
  • Grammar:
    • using "isn't it?" for all question tags ("You are coming, isn't it?" → "You are coming, aren't you?")
    • "He is having two children" → "He has two children"
    • "Myself Rahul" → "I am Rahul"
  • Fillers and a flat tone – "umm", "actually", "basically"; monotonous speech

Correction: listening to good models (news readers, dictionaries with audio), recording and listening to oneself, minimal-pair practice (vet/wet, ship/sip), reading aloud, role plays and presentations with feedback.

C. Errors in reading

  • Word-by-word reading and sub-vocalisation – slow reading
  • Misreading drug names, doses and decimal points – reading "5.0 mg" as 50 mg, or ".5 mg" as 5 mg (hence "always put a zero before a decimal (0.5 mg) and never put a zero after it (5 mg, not 5.0 mg)")
  • Skipping instructions or reading only part of a question in examinations
  • Not understanding vocabulary, idioms and abbreviations
  • Uncritical reading – believing everything printed or forwarded

Correction: intensive reading of important documents, reading in phrases, building vocabulary, the SQ3R method, reading the full question twice, and critical reading of sources.

D. Errors in writing

  • Spelling:
    • recieve → receive
    • seperate → separate
    • accomodation → accommodation
    • occured → occurred
    • untill → until
    • dieases → diseases
  • Confusing words: affect / effect, advice (noun) / advise (verb), practice (noun) / practise (verb), principal / principle, loose / lose, its / it's
  • Articles: "a hour" → "an hour"; "an uniform" → "a uniform" (articles depend on sound, not letter)
  • Subject–verb agreement: "The list of patients are ready" → "The list of patients is ready"
  • Tense errors: "I have completed my GNM in 2020" → "I completed my GNM in 2020"
  • Punctuation: run-on sentences, missing full stops, wrong apostrophes
  • Sentence fragments and very long, unclear sentences
  • Illegible handwriting and unapproved abbreviations in records – e.g. "U" for units read as "0"

Correction: proofreading, using a dictionary, keeping a list of one's own frequent errors, writing practice with feedback, peer review, learning grammar rules, using approved abbreviations and writing legibly.

Summary table

Skill Common errors Remedy
Listening missed numbers, sound-alike words read-back, ask for repetition, write down
Speaking v/w, extra vowels, wrong stress, "isn't it?" model listening, recording, drills
Reading slow reading, decimal misreading phrase reading, intensive reading, SQ3R
Writing spelling, articles, agreement, abbreviations proofreading, dictionary, feedback

Importance in nursing

  • Errors in listening, reading and writing orders, doses and records can directly harm patients; error analysis helps prevent them

Conclusion Error analysis identifies, classifies and explains the errors learners make in listening, speaking, reading and writing. Most errors come from mother-tongue influence, over-generalisation, incomplete learning and carelessness. With regular practice, feedback, self-correction and safety habits such as read-back and correct decimal writing, nurses can communicate accurately and safely.

question: Write four instructions for a patient going home after cataract surgery.
answer_html:
Instructions

  1. Put the eye drops exactly as prescribed, after washing your hands.
  2. Wear the protective shield at night and dark glasses outdoors, as advised.
  3. Do not rub or press the operated eye, and do not let water or soap enter it while bathing.

subject: Communicative English
question: Write instructions for a patient on how to collect a midstream urine sample.
answer_html:
How to Collect a Midstream Urine Sample

Purpose: to test your urine for infection without contamination from the skin.

You will need: a sterile container with a lid (given by the hospital) and a label.

Steps

  1. Wash your hands with soap and water.
  2. Open the container carefully. Do not touch the inside of the container or the lid. Place the lid with its inner side facing up.
  3. Clean the genital area with clean water:
    • Women – separate the labia and wipe from front to back.
    • Men – pull back the foreskin (if present) and clean the tip of the penis.
  4. Start passing urine into the toilet and let the first part flow away.
  5. Without stopping the flow, collect the middle part of the urine in the container, filling it about halfway.
  6. Pass the rest of the urine into the toilet.
  7. Close the lid tightly.
  8. Wash your hands again.
  9. Write or check the label – your name, date and time.
  10. Hand over the container to the nurse or laboratory within one hour. If there is a delay, keep it in a refrigerator, not a freezer.

Important

  • An early morning sample is best, unless told otherwise.
  • Women should tell the nurse if they are menstruating.
  • Parents should help young children.

Language features of good instructions

  • A clear title and purpose
  • Numbered steps in the correct order
  • Each step begins with an imperative verb – wash, open, clean, collect
  • Sequence words where needed – first, then, next, finally
  • Simple vocabulary; one action per step
  • Warnings and important points highlighted
  • Pictures or diagrams may be added for patients who cannot read

Why the midstream sample?

  • The first part of the stream washes away germs from the urethra and skin; the middle part better represents the urine in the bladder, so the test result is more reliable

Note for nurses: in a patient with a urinary catheter, the sample is taken by the nurse from the sampling port of the catheter tubing using aseptic technique – never from the drainage bag.

subject: Communicative English
question: Write a report on a fire mock drill conducted in your hospital.
answer_html:
FIRE MOCK DRILL CONDUCTED IN THE HOSPITAL

Reported by: Ward Sister, Surgical Ward Date: 15 November 2026

Introduction A fire mock drill was conducted in the hospital on 14 November 2026 at 11 am, under the guidance of the Medical Superintendent and the fire safety officer of the municipal fire brigade. Its aim was to test the preparedness of staff to respond to a fire and to evacuate patients safely.

Details of the drill At 11.00 am, a mock fire was announced in the store room of the surgical ward. The staff nurse on duty raised the alarm by breaking the glass of the fire alarm point and informed the telephone operator, who announced a "Code Red" over the public address system. Nurses followed the RACE procedure. Patients in the area nearest to the store room were moved first. Walking patients were guided out, and bed-bound patients were shifted by wheelchairs and stretchers to the safe area beyond the fire doors. The fire safety officer then demonstrated the use of ABC and CO₂ extinguishers using the PASS method, and several staff members practised using them.

Observations

  • The alarm was raised within one minute.
  • All 28 patients of the ward were evacuated in six minutes.
  • Some staff did not know the location of the oxygen zone valve.
  • One fire exit was partly blocked by old furniture.

Recommendations

  1. Training on the location and use of oxygen zone valves for all nursing staff.
  2. Immediate removal of furniture blocking the fire exit.
  3. Mock drills to be conducted regularly in every ward, including the night shift.

Conclusion The drill was useful and showed good teamwork. With the suggested improvements, the hospital will be better prepared to protect patients in a real emergency.

(Signature) Ward Sister, Surgical Ward

Features of a good report

  • A clear title, reporter's name and date
  • Introduction – what, when, where and why
  • Body in time order, in the past tense, often in the passive voice
  • Facts and figures; observations kept separate from recommendations
  • Recommendations and conclusion; signature
